description: Per-translation overlay glossary for the Gospel of Thomas (Nag Hammadi Codex II,2), the program's first Coptic-source text. v1.0.0 covers Block A (incipit and logia 1-38) and fixes the conventions that bind Blocks B and C: modern register and saying format; the restored-text bracket rule ([ ] for English words standing on restored letters; ⟨ ⟩ and ( ) source sigla rendered silently; the source file kept immutable and its anomalies recorded in commentary); silent expansion of nomina sacra; Greek loanwords translated, not transliterated; and the Coptic as base text with the Oxyrhynchus Greek (P.Oxy. 1, 654, 655) in commentary only. Lexical decisions: hidden sayings, the living (lower case), Didymos Judas Thomas, interpretation, not taste death, the All, the kingdom (and 'domain' at 21), ⲧⲡⲉ sky/heaven by context, sons/children, Father capitalisation, poverty, a single one, place, ⲣⲱⲙⲉ, the singular beatitude, the lion crux (manuscript kept), Thomas's sower, world/earth, light, James the Righteous, the vocabulary of logion 13, spirit/flesh/body, born of woman, solitary ones (monachos), beginning/end, five trees in Paradise, Mariham, the robbers clause of 21, image, soul, fasting from the world and the Sabbath, the three-gods crux (manuscript kept), and the ear/measure crux of 33. One speculative entry records the Wheel of Heaven reading of logia 3, 18 and 19 as apparatus only. Indexing: Coptic has no Strong's numbers; the 'strongs' field carries Crum, A Coptic Dictionary (1939) headwords and, for Greek loans, the Strong's G-number of the Greek word. Cross-corpus changes (adding 'cop' to the central sourceLanguages; appliesTo extensions of central entries) are proposed in chapter-1-editor-report.md, not applied here. v1.1.0 (Block B, logia 39-76): adds the whole-word supply convention (English ⟨ ⟩ for an editor-supplied word, THOM-60) and lexical entries for knowledge (gnosis), passers-by, the Jews, the triad of 44, bad/evil, slave/master/lord, chosen, movement/repose/rest, the vocabulary of 50, John's eyes (46), corpse, the darnel parable, suffered, look to / watch out for, the Samaritan crux (60), Salome, the one who is equal and the crux of 61, mysteries, the dinner parable, the vineyard restoration and crux (65), lacking entirely (67), the persecution beatitudes (68-69), destroy and build (71), divider (72), the trough/sickness crux (74, '(?)' on 'drinking trough' only), the bridal chamber, the merchant and pearl with 'his treasure' (76), the twenty-four prophets (52) and circumcision in spirit (53). One speculative entry records the Wheel of Heaven reading of logion 50 as apparatus only. Ratified Block A entries are unchanged except for appliesTo extensions and a new scopeNote field. v1.2.0 (Block C, logia 77-114): adds two conventions (focalising conversions rendered as English clefts where the focus is a contrasted adverbial; restored morphs that no English word renders produce no bracket, and extant letters never stand inside one) and the subscript-title entry ('The Gospel according to Thomas', carried in translation.subscriptTitle, not as a unit); lexical entries for logion 77 (the light above all; the ⲡⲱϩ reach/split catchword), countryside / shaken / great men (78, 98), the native beatitude ⲛⲁⲓⲁⲧ= and λόγος 'the word of the Father' (79), renounce / power (81, 85, 110), manifest / revealed / appear (83, 84, 108), likeness and images (84), worthy (80, 85, 111, 114), depend on / wretched / woe (87, 102, 112), angels and prophets (88), made (89), the easy yoke and lordship (90), test the face of the sky (91), the holy-to-dogs saying and its gap (93), money at interest (95, 109), the leaven, jar and assassin parables (96-98), God and Caesar (100), hate/love and the true mother (101), the dog in the manger (102, inferred), the householder's 'domain' at 103 (inferred; extends the logion-21 exception), bridegroom and bridal chamber (104, recording the loan/native pair with 75), the son of a whore (105), sons of man (106), the shepherd (107), drinking from the mouth (108), the hidden treasure (109), the living one and the closing gloss (111, inferred), the kingdom spread upon the earth (113) and 'make her male' kept in the manuscript reading (114). One speculative entry records the Wheel of Heaven reading of logion 88 as apparatus only. Ratified Block A and Block B entries are unchanged except for appliesTo extensions and scopeNote additions.

entries.partOfSpeech: convention: English register, saying format, speaker attribution and proper-name forms
entries.literal: (not applicable — meta)
entries.standardEnglish: Modern scholarly translations (Lambdin in Layton ed. 1989; Patterson–Meyer; Plisch 2008) use a plain modern register, introduce each saying with 'Jesus said', and vary between Latinised and Greek name forms
entries.wohChoice: Modern English register as in matthew-woh (you/your; no archaisms). Each saying keeps the manuscript's own introduction (ⲡⲉϫⲉ ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ 'Jesus said:'), with a colon and no quotation marks around the saying itself; quoted speech inside a saying takes single quotes. No introduction is supplied where the Coptic has none (logion 27). 'And he said' (logion 1) keeps the manuscript's unresolved speaker. The sayings keep their terseness; hard sayings are not smoothed toward the canonical gospels. Proper names: Jesus, Didymos Judas Thomas, Simon Peter, Matthew, Thomas, Mariham, James the Righteous (see the name entries).
entries.rationale: The program's NT translations (matthew-woh, mark-woh, luke-woh) use a modern scholarly register, and the Translator's draft already followed it; this entry fixes that register for all three blocks of Thomas so that Blocks B and C cannot drift. Thomas is a sayings collection whose meaning often depends on compression and paradox, so the convention forbids harmonising toward the synoptic wording: where the Coptic is short (logion 36), odd (logion 7, 30) or abrupt (logion 27, no introductory formula), the English keeps that shape and the apparatus explains it. The speaker of logion 1 is grammatically open in both the Coptic (ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ) and the Greek of P.Oxy. 654.3 (καὶ εἶπεν): the antecedent may be Jesus or the compiler named in the incipit, and modern editions differ, so the English does not resolve it. No lens is carried by this convention.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): applied to logia 39-76. No formula is supplied where the Coptic lacks one: Jesus's answer at 43 and Salome's reply 'I am your disciple' at 61 run on (the 61 case is escalated for review); 65 keeps the manuscript's 'He said'; 72 opens 'A [man said] to him'. Proper names added: Salome (see `salome-name-thomas-woh`), John the Baptist, Adam, Israel, Judea. v1.2.0 (Block C): applied to logia 77-114. No formula is supplied where the Coptic lacks one: 93 (may continue 92), 101, and the answer in 113 run on as at 43; 95 prints the wholly restored '[Jesus said:]'. Proper names added: Adam (85), Caesar (100), Simon Peter and Mariham (114); 'the Pharisees' as at 39 (102). The subscript title is carried in `translation.subscriptTitle` (see `subscript-title-gospel-according-to-thomas-thomas-woh`).

entries.source: [ ] ⟨ ⟩ ( ) { } in the Dilley edition (orig_group layer of source-cop-1.json)
entries.partOfSpeech: convention: rendering of editorial restorations, additions and supplied letters
entries.literal: Dilley's sigla: [ ] lacuna restored; ⟨ ⟩ editorial addition (letter omitted by the scribe); ( ) resolved abbreviation or supplied letter; { } scribal surplus
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin (in Layton ed. 1989) marks restorations; most popular translations print them silently
entries.wohChoice: Three rules, one function each. (1) Square brackets [ ] enclose any English word whose Coptic token is wholly or partly restored inside [ ] in the source (THOM-8 '[down]', 16 '[be]', 22 '[the kingdom]', 29 '[how]', 37 '[then you will]'). (2) ⟨ ⟩ additions and ( ) supplied letters in the source correct scribal slips or resolve abbreviations; they fill no physical gap and are rendered silently in the English, with the Coptic form visible in `text` and, where it affects the reading, noted in commentary (THOM-9, 13, 14, 20, 27, 36). (3) An unrestorable gap would be printed '…' (none in Block A). The English angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ are reserved, as in vendidad-woh, for English words supplied by the Editor where no Coptic wording exists; none are used in Block A. The source file stays immutable: where the corpus's normalised layer supplies or corrects letters that the diplomatic `text` does not mark (THOM-3, 10, 18, and the span-count mismatches at 8 and 22), the English follows the normalised reading and the finding is recorded in commentary and in the Editor report.
entries.rationale: This adopts the central `lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard` distinction between restoration [word] and editorial supply ⟨word⟩, as applied in vendidad-woh, and maps it onto the Leiden-style sigla of Dilley's papyrological edition. Thomas has a single complete witness (NHC II,2), so every [ ] in the Coptic is a modern restoration of a physical lacuna in that witness, most of them secure from context; the reader is nevertheless entitled to see which English words stand on restored letters, and partial restorations are bracketed for the same reason, because the convention must be mechanical to be auditable. The ⟨ ⟩ and ( ) sigla, by contrast, mark letters the scribe omitted or abbreviated (ⲉⲉ⟨ⲓ⟩ⲛⲉ, ϣⲟ(ⲛ)ⲧⲉ), and bracketing whole English words for a one-letter scribal slip would misrepresent the text as damaged. Block B and C restorations (notably in the damaged lower margins of the codex pages) follow the same three rules.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): (a) rule 2 is limited to supplied letters; a ⟨ ⟩ supply of a whole word is printed in English angle brackets under `whole-word-supply-angle-brackets-convention-thomas-woh` (THOM-60). (b) Adjacent bracketed English words share one bracket pair (THOM-71, 72, as at THOM-37). (c) Double square brackets [[ ]] mark a scribal erasure (THOM-63), not a restoration, and produce no English bracket. (d) Negative optatives written defectively in the manuscript (single ⲛ, THOM-59 as at 21/22) or supplied only in the normalised layer (THOM-46) are read as negatives without brackets. (e) Where { } deletes a meaningful morpheme that the scribe's own correction presupposes (THOM-76 ⲡ{ⲉϥ}), convention 6 (manuscript reading stands) governs and the deletion is reported in commentary. (f) Unrestored gap printed '…' for the first time at THOM-71. v1.2.0 (Block C): rule 1 is applied at morph level; restored morphs with no English word produce no bracket, and extant (underdotted) letters never stand inside a bracket (see `restored-morph-without-english-word-convention-thomas-woh`; corrections at 97, 103, 109). Adjacent bracketed words merged at 78 ('[man who]') and 93 ('[pearls to]'). [[ ]] scribal erasures at 79 and 107 produce no bracket (as at 63). Silent sigla: { } and ⟨ ⟩ correcting the metathesis in ⲁⲛⲁ{ⲩ}ⲡⲁ⟨ⲩ⟩ⲥⲓⲥ (90); ( ) at 101, 103, 107. Unrestored gaps printed '…' at 93 and 101 (two). The duplicated ϯ̣ⲡ̣[ⲉ in the `text` of 85 is read once.

entries.partOfSpeech: convention: scribal contractions with supralinear stroke
entries.literal: contracted names and words marked by an overline
entries.standardEnglish: All standard English translations expand nomina sacra silently ('Jesus', 'spirit')
entries.wohChoice: Expand silently in the English, with no typographic marking; the contracted forms and their overlines stay visible in the `text` field. Non-sacral overlined contractions are likewise expanded silently.
entries.rationale: The nomina sacra are a scribal convention shared by Greek and Coptic Christian manuscripts and are not part of the wording: ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ is read 'Jesus' by every edition, and no translation marks it. Marking them in English (small capitals, notes on every saying) would turn a feature of the manuscript's writing system into a claim about meaning, which the Translation Program reserves for the apparatus. Overlines on ordinary words (ⲧⲃ︤ⲧ︥ 'fish', ϩⲏⲃ︤ⲥ︥ 'lamp') are the same scribal habit and are treated the same way. The `text` field preserves every overline, so the convention loses nothing for a reader of the Coptic.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): the staurogram (tau-rho ligature) in ⲙⲡⲉϥⲥⳁⲟⲥ (THOM-55) is expanded silently to 'cross' under this convention; the `text` field keeps the ligature. On the staurogram see Hurtado, The Earliest Christian Artifacts (2006). v1.2.0 (Block C): ⲓ︤ⲥ︥ / ⲓⲏ︤ⲥ︥ (90) expanded silently, including the restored [ⲡⲉϫⲉⲓ︤ⲥ︥ ϫⲉ] at 95 and the form ⲓⲥ written without overline at 94 (source finding); ⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥ 'spirit' (114); overlined contractions ⲧⲁⲙⲛ︤ⲧ︥ϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ (90), ⲧⲙ︤ⲛ︥ⲧⲉⲣⲟ (96), ϭⲗ︦ⲙⲉⲉⲓ (97), ⲙⲛ︤ⲧ︥ⲉⲣⲟ (103), ⲙ︤ⲡ︥ⲉϥ (109) and the scribal stroke in ⲛⲉⲉⲓⲁⲧϥ︦ (79) expanded or ignored silently.

entries.strongs: Förster, Wörterbuch der griechischen Wörter in den koptischen dokumentarischen Texten (2002); Coptic Scriptorium loanword tags
entries.literal: Greek words embedded in the Coptic sentence
entries.standardEnglish: Translated into ordinary English in all standard translations
entries.wohChoice: Translate every loanword into ordinary English; no loanword is transliterated or typographically marked in the English. Where the choice of the loan carries meaning (ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ beside native ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ; ⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ beside native ⲙⲁ; ⲁⲣⲭⲏ beside native ϩⲁⲏ) the distinction is recorded in that lemma's entry and in commentary.
entries.rationale: Greek loanwords are a normal part of Sahidic Coptic vocabulary, used by Coptic speakers as Coptic words, and a Coptic reader would not have heard ⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ or ⲯⲩⲭⲏ as foreign. Transliterating selected loans (monachos, topos, archē) would make the English look more technical than the Coptic is and would suggest a Greek Vorlage reading at points where the Coptic is our only witness. Where a loan sits next to a native synonym and the pair matters, the apparatus records it, so nothing is lost for the reader who wants it.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): further meaningful loan/native pairs are recorded in their entries: ⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ 'repose' vs ⲙ̄ⲧⲟⲛ 'rest'; ⲕⲁⲕⲟⲥ/ⲡⲟⲛⲏⲣⲟⲛ vs ϩⲟⲟⲩ; ⲱⲫⲉⲗⲉⲓ 'useful' vs ϭⲛ̄ϩⲏⲩ 'profitable'; ⲉⲙⲡⲟⲣⲟⲥ vs ⲉϣⲱⲧ (both 'merchants'); ⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ 'corpse' vs ⲥⲱⲙⲁ 'body'; ⲅⲛⲱⲥⲓⲥ 'knowledge'. v1.2.0 (Block C): loan/native pairs recorded in their entries: ⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ vs ⲛⲁⲓⲁⲧ= (both 'Blessed'); ⲗⲟⲅⲟⲥ 'word' vs ϣⲁϫⲉ 'sayings'; ⲁⲝⲓⲟⲥ vs ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ (both 'worthy'); ⲛⲩⲙⲫⲱⲛ vs ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ (both 'the bridal chamber'); ϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ 'image' vs ⲉⲓⲛⲉ 'likeness'; ⲧⲁⲗⲁⲓⲡⲱⲣⲟⲥ 'wretched' vs ⲟⲩⲟⲓ 'woe'; ⲁⲛⲁⲡⲁⲩⲥⲓⲥ 'repose' vs ⲙ̄ⲧⲟⲛ 'rest'. entries.source: NHC II,2 (Coptic, 4th c.) vs P.Oxy. 654 (incipit–7), P.Oxy. 1 (26–33, 77b), P.Oxy. 655 (24, 36–39)
entries.strongs: Grenfell & Hunt, The Oxyrhynchus Papyri I (1898) and IV (1904); Attridge, 'The Greek Fragments', in Layton (ed.), Nag Hammadi Codex II,2-7, vol. 1 (NHS 20; Brill 1989); Fitzmyer, Theological Studies 20 (1959)
entries.partOfSpeech: convention: base text and treatment of the Greek witnesses
entries.literal: (not applicable — meta)
entries.standardEnglish: Most English translations of the Gospel of Thomas translate the Coptic and print the Greek fragments separately or in notes; some synopses translate the Greek where it is extant
entries.wohChoice: The English translates the Coptic of NHC II,2 throughout. The Greek of the Oxyrhynchus fragments is never imported into the English line; every material Greek–Coptic divergence is recorded in that unit's commentary, with restored Greek identified as restored. Where the Coptic is longer, shorter or different (2 'troubled'/'rest'; 3 'sea'/'under the earth'; 6 'heaven'/'truth'; 27 'kingdom'/'kingdom of God'; 30; 31 'village'/'homeland'; 36 short/long form), the Coptic stands in the line.
entries.rationale: The Greek fragments are earlier (third century; P.Oxy. 1 is commonly dated around 200) than the fourth-century Coptic codex, but they are fragmentary and represent a different recension: the two forms differ in wording, length and sometimes order (P.Oxy. 1 joins 30 and 77b), so neither can be corrected from the other without choosing a recension, which is a text-critical claim the translation does not make. The project translates one witness consistently and makes the other fully visible, which is also the practice of the major critical editions that print the two side by side (Layton ed. 1989 with Attridge; Plisch 2008). Much of the Greek is restored (the incipit's 'secret', logion 3's 'of God', logion 30's 'without God'), so commentary always flags restored Greek as such.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): THOM-39 is the last Block B unit with a Greek overlap (P.Oxy. 655 col. ii, largely restored; no secure divergence). Logia 40-76 have no Greek witness. v1.2.0 (Block C): THOM-77 is the only Block C unit with a Greek overlap: P.Oxy. 1.27-30 has 77b (stone first, then wood; definite 'the wood'; ἔγειρον 'raise') attached to logion 30 and lacks 77a. The Coptic order and placement stand; the ⲡⲱϩ catchword that joins 77a and 77b is Coptic-only.

entries.source: ⲛ̄ϣⲁϫⲉ ⲉⲑⲏⲡ (ϣⲁϫⲉ + ⲉⲧ-ϩⲏⲡ)
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϣⲁϫⲉ; s.v. ϩⲱⲡ (stative ϩⲏⲡ); Greek P.Oxy. 654.1 οἱ λόγοι οἱ [ἀπόκρυφοι] (adjective restored); λόγος G3056; ἀπόκρυφος G614
entries.lemma: ϣⲁϫⲉ 'word, saying, speech'; ϩⲱⲡ 'hide' (stative ϩⲏⲡ 'be hidden')
entries.literal: the words which are hidden
entries.standardEnglish: 'the secret sayings' (Lambdin); 'the hidden sayings' (Meyer 1992; Patterson–Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'the hidden sayings'. ϣⲁϫⲉ = 'sayings' where it denotes the sayings of the collection (THOM-0, 1, 19, 38); 'words' for speech in narrative (THOM-13 'three words', 'one of the words'). ϩⲏⲡ = 'hidden' at every occurrence (THOM-0, 5, 6, 33).
entries.rationale: ϩⲏⲡ is the stative of ϩⲱⲡ 'hide', so 'hidden' is the literal rendering; 'secret' (Lambdin) translates the restored Greek ἀπόκρυφοι rather than the Coptic, and the Coptic is our base text. Rendering ϩⲏⲡ as 'hidden' at every occurrence keeps the incipit audible in logia 5 and 6 ('what is hidden from you will be revealed'), a link the collection appears to build deliberately. 'Sayings' for ϣⲁϫⲉ matches the genre (a logia collection, Greek λόγοι) and the established English title of the text; in narrative (logion 13) 'words' is the natural English for the same noun.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): the active verb ϩⲱⲡ 'hide' is rendered with the same root ('have hidden them', THOM-39). v1.2.0 (Block C): stative ϩⲏⲡ 'hidden' (83, 109); ⲛⲉⲑⲏⲡ 'the hidden things' (108); active ϩⲱⲡ 'hid' (96).

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲱⲛϩ (stative ⲟⲛϩ); Greek P.Oxy. 654.1 ὁ ζῶν; ζάω G2198
entries.literal: Jesus who is alive; the Father who is alive; the one who is alive
entries.standardEnglish: 'the living Jesus' (all standard translations); 'the son of the living one' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: Lower case throughout: 'the living Jesus' (THOM-0), 'the living Father' (THOM-3), 'the living' / 'what is alive' (THOM-11), 'the son of the living one' (THOM-37). No title capitalisation ('the Living One') is introduced in Block A; the substantive recurs at logia 52, 59, 111 (Blocks B/C) and follows the same rule.
entries.rationale: ⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ is an ordinary relative stative ('who is alive'), used of Jesus, of the Father, of the disciples' state and of food in the same block, and Coptic has no capitalisation to signal a title. Capitalising 'the Living One' at THOM-37 would make the English assert a fixed divine title where the Coptic offers only the participle, and would sever the visible link with 'the living Father' (3) and 'the living' (11). Whether 'the living Jesus' means the risen Jesus or the one who has life is debated in the commentaries, and the lower-case rendering leaves that question open, as the Greek ὁ ζῶν does.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'the living Father' (50), 'the living one' (52, 59), lower case. v1.2.0 (Block C): 'the living one' (111, the substantive; the first ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ there is verbal, 'the one who lives from', see `logion-111-the-living-one-and-gloss-thomas-woh`); 'a living spirit' (114).

entries.strongs: G1324 (Δίδυμος); G2455 (Ἰούδας); G2381 (Θωμᾶς); Aramaic tᵓōmā 'twin'
entries.literal: the Twin, Judas, the Twin
entries.standardEnglish: 'Didymos Judas Thomas' (Lambdin; Meyer); 'Didymus Judas Thomas' (older Latinised form)
entries.wohChoice: 'Didymos Judas Thomas' (Greek form of Didymos, the familiar English 'Judas' and 'Thomas'); 'Thomas' in logion 13. Neither by-name is translated in the line; the double meaning 'twin' is explained in commentary.
entries.rationale: Didymos (Greek δίδυμος) and Thomas (Aramaic tᵓōmā) both mean 'twin', and the triple name is the form under which the apostle is known in Syrian tradition (Acts of Thomas; the Book of Thomas, NHC II,7). Translating either by-name ('Judas the Twin') would turn a proper name into a description and hide the bilingual doubling that is itself evidence for the text's milieu. The Greek incipit (P.Oxy. 654.2-3) reads, as restored, 'Judas who is also Thomas', without Didymos; this is recorded in commentary, and the Greek form 'Didymos' is preferred to the Latinised 'Didymus' because the Coptic spells the Greek word.

entries.standardEnglish: 'the interpretation' (Lambdin; Meyer; Patterson–Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'finds the interpretation of these sayings'
entries.rationale: ἑρμηνεία means 'interpretation, explanation, translation', and every standard translation renders it 'interpretation'. 'Meaning' would shift the emphasis from an act of understanding that the reader must perform to a property of the text, which is less exact. The verb ϩⲉ ⲉ- 'find' (Lycopolitan ⲡⲉⲧⲁϩⲉ for Sahidic ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁϩⲉ) is kept literal because 'seek' and 'find' are the collection's governing pair (logion 2).

entries.source: ϥⲛⲁϫⲓϯⲡⲉ ⲁⲛ ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲟⲩ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϫⲓ ϯⲡⲉ 'taste'; Greek γεύσηται θανάτου (P.Oxy. 654.5, restored); γεύομαι G1089; θάνατος G2288
entries.literal: he will not taste death
entries.standardEnglish: 'will not taste death' (all standard translations of Thomas; Mt 16:28 / Mk 9:1 / Jn 8:52 in KJV-RSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'will not taste death' at every occurrence (THOM-1, 18, 19; later 85). Logion 111 has a different verb, ϥⲛⲁⲛⲁⲩ ⲁⲛ ⲉⲙⲟⲩ, rendered 'will not see death'.
entries.rationale: The phrase is a Semitic idiom that the synoptic and Johannine tradition also uses (Mt 16:28; Mk 9:1; Lk 9:27; Jn 8:52), and English readers recognise it in that form. Rendering it 'will not die' or 'will not experience death' would erase the idiom and the intertextual link the Coptic preserves. A single rendering at every occurrence lets the reader see that the promise of logion 1 recurs as a refrain through the collection.
entries.scopeNote: v1.2.0 (Block C): at 85 the idiom is kept and the tense follows the Coptic: the preterite future ⲛⲉϥⲛⲁϫⲓϯⲡⲉ ⲁⲛ in the apodosis of an unreal condition is 'he would not have tasted death' (ruled at Block A sign-off: '85 taste death'). At 111 the verb is ⲛⲁⲩ 'see', not this idiom: 'will not see death' (corrected at Block A sign-off); 111 is listed here only to record that contrast.

entries.source: ϥⲛⲁⲣ̄ⲣ̄ⲣⲟ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲧⲏⲣ= 'all, whole' (substantive ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ 'the All'); s.v. ⲣ̄ⲣⲟ 'be king'; Greek P.Oxy. 654.8 βασιλεύσει (no object); βασιλεύω G936
entries.literal: he will become king over the entirety
entries.standardEnglish: 'he will rule over the All' (Lambdin); 'the entirety' or 'all' in other translations
entries.wohChoice: 'he will reign over the All' — 'the All' capitalised as a technical substantive, here and at its later occurrences (logia 67, 77). ⲣ̄ⲣⲣⲟ = 'reign'.
entries.rationale: ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ ('the whole', masculine article + ⲧⲏⲣ= with resumptive suffix) is a set term in Coptic Nag Hammadi texts for the totality of what exists, and Lambdin's 'the All' is the established English for it. Capitalising it marks it as a substantive and keeps it recognisable at 67 and 77 ('I am the All'), where lower-case 'all' would be misread as a quantifier. ⲣ̄ⲣⲣⲟ is literally 'become king'; 'reign' keeps the royal sense that 'rule' weakens, and matches the Greek βασιλεύσει.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'the All' at THOM-67, as anticipated. v1.2.0 (Block C): 'I am the All … the All came forth … the All has reached' (77, as anticipated); ⲣ̄ⲣⲣⲟ 'reign' (81).

entries.source: ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ (ⲧ-ⲙⲛ̄ⲧ-ⲉⲣⲟ); ⲧⲉϥⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲣⲣⲟ (abstract ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ 'kingship, kingdom'); Greek βασιλεία G932
entries.literal: the kingship / the kingdom
entries.standardEnglish: 'the kingdom' (all standard translations); 'his domain' at logion 21 (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'the kingdom' for absolute ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ (THOM-3, 22, 27; later blocks); 'the kingdom of the heavens' for ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲛ̄ⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ (THOM-20, under the central Matthean entry); 'the kingdom of the Father' when it occurs (logia 57, 76, 96 ff.). One exception by context: in the householder image of logion 21, ⲉⲡⲉϥⲏⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉ ⲧⲉϥⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ is rendered 'into his house of his domain' (Lambdin), with the identity of the word noted in commentary.
entries.rationale: ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ is the Coptic abstract of ⲣⲣⲟ 'king' and is the standard rendering of βασιλεία; 'kingdom' is the near-universal English for both and keeps Thomas's kingdom sayings recognisable beside the synoptic ones. 'Kingship' or 'reign' are defensible, but would make Thomas look more abstract than the synoptics when the Coptic word is the same one used to translate them. At logion 21 the word describes a householder's own property, where 'kingdom' would read as a deliberate allegory that the Coptic does not mark; Lambdin's 'domain' gives the plain sense, and commentary keeps the lexical identity visible.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'the kingdom' (46, 49), 'the kingdom of the heavens' (54, central entry), 'the kingdom of the Father' (57, 76). v1.2.0 (Block C): 'the kingdom' (82, 107, 109, 113); 'the kingdom of the Father' (96, 97, 98, 113); 'the kingdom of my Father' (99); 'the kingdom of the heavens' (114, central entry). The logion-21 exception applies by its own criterion to the identical householder-and-robbers image of 103: 'gather his [domain]' (see `logion-103-householder-domain-and-robbers-thomas-woh`, inferred; escalated for review).

entries.source: ⲧⲡⲉ (sg.); ⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ (pl.)
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲡⲉ 'heaven, sky' (pl. ⲡⲏⲩⲉ); Greek οὐρανός G3772
entries.literal: the sky / heaven
entries.standardEnglish: 'heaven' in most contexts, 'sky' in logion 3 (Lambdin and Patterson–Meyer: 'the kingdom is in the sky … the birds of the sky')
entries.wohChoice: One word, rendered by context, with concordance kept inside each saying. 'the sky' in physical contexts: THOM-3 ('the kingdom is in the sky … the birds of the sky', the saying's joke depends on the same word), THOM-9 ('ears toward the sky', 'fruit up toward the sky'), THOM-20 ('the birds of the sky', as matthew-woh 6:26 and 13:32). 'heaven' in cosmological and theological contexts: THOM-6 ('in the sight of heaven'), THOM-11 ('this heaven will pass away, and the one above it'), THOM-12 ('heaven and earth'). Plural ⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ = 'the heavens' (THOM-20).
entries.rationale: Coptic ⲡⲉ, like Greek οὐρανός and Hebrew šāmayim, covers both the visible sky and heaven as a cosmological or divine realm, so English must choose by context. The draft's 'heaven' everywhere spoiled logion 3, whose point is that a kingdom located 'in the sky' would be reached first by birds; 'sky' there is both more literal and the reading of Lambdin and Patterson–Meyer, and matthew-woh already renders 'the birds of the sky'. Where the context is cosmological (11: a layered heaven 'and the one above it') or a fixed pair (12: 'heaven and earth'), 'heaven' is kept. The split is an editorial judgement about context rather than a lexical fact, hence `inferred`; it carries no lens, and it is not adjusted toward the central Hebrew choice 'skies' for šāmayim, which belongs to a different source language.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'neither on earth nor in heaven' (44, cosmological pair); plural ⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ 'the heavens' (54). v1.2.0 (Block C): 'the face of the sky and the earth' (91, weather image, physical); plural ⲙ̄ⲡⲏⲩⲉ 'the heavens' (111 'the heavens will be rolled up'; 114 'the kingdom of the heavens').

entries.source: ϣⲏⲣⲉ; ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ; ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲛ̄ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ; ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ; ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϣⲏⲣⲉ 'son, child'; s.v. ϣⲏⲙ 'small'; Greek υἱοί (P.Oxy. 654.17, partly restored); υἱοῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων (P.Oxy. 1.20); υἱός G5207
entries.literal: son / child
entries.standardEnglish: 'sons of the living father', 'sons of men' (Lambdin); 'children of the living Father', 'children of humanity' (Patterson–Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'sons' in the filial formulas (ϣⲏⲣⲉ + genitive of the Father, of humanity, or of 'the living one'): 'the sons of the living Father' (THOM-3), 'the sons of men' (THOM-28), 'the son of the living one' (THOM-37). 'little child(ren)' for ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ / ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ (THOM-4, 21, 37); 'little ones' for substantival ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ (THOM-22).
entries.rationale: ϣⲏⲣⲉ is common-gender in Coptic ('son' or 'child'), so either English is lexically possible. For the filial formulas the earlier Greek, where it survives, has υἱοῖς (P.Oxy. 1 at 28, extant) and is restored with υἱοί at 3 (P.Oxy. 654); at 37 the Greek is lost, and 'sons of men' is the established English for the Semitic idiom behind υἱοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων; 'sons' therefore represents both witnesses most exactly and keeps the phrase aligned with matthew-woh ('sons of your Father', Mt 5:45). Where the reference is to small children (ϣⲏⲣⲉ ϣⲏⲙ, 'little child'), gender is not in view and 'child' is used. The inclusive alternative ('children of the living Father') is noted in the Editor report as a register question for the human reviewer, not adopted here. Ruled at human sign-off (2026-11-01): "sons" kept in the filial formulas for the whole book.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'its sons' (50, filial formula with the light as antecedent); predicative ⲉϥⲟ ⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ 'becomes a little one' (46); 'his son' / 'my son' in the parable (65, literal). Absolute ⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ in the triad of 44 is capitalised 'the Son' under `son-and-holy-spirit-triad-logion-44-thomas-woh`. v1.2.0 (Block C): 'the son of a whore' (105, filial formula); plural 'sons of man' (106, lower case; not the central title); 'his son', 'the son' (109, literal). The singular ⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ at 86 is 'the Son of Man' under the central Son-of-Man convention.

entries.source: ⲡⲉⲓⲱⲧ; ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓⲱⲧ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲉⲓⲱⲧ 'father'; Greek πατήρ G3962 (P.Oxy. 654.17, 1.11)
entries.literal: the father
entries.standardEnglish: 'father' lower case (Lambdin); 'Father' (Patterson–Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'Father' capitalised where the referent is the divine Father: 'the living Father' (THOM-3), 'your Father' (THOM-15), 'the Father' (THOM-27), and 'the kingdom of the Father' in later blocks. Lower case for a human father (THOM-16 'the father against the son').
entries.rationale: Coptic has no capitalisation, so this is an English typographic convention, and the program's NT translations already follow it (matthew-woh: 'your Father who is in the heavens', 'our Father'). Keeping the same convention lets readers move between the synoptic and the Thomas sayings without an apparent difference that is not in the sources. The human father of logion 16 (Mt 10:35 parallel) is lower case, so the capital is reserved for one referent and stays meaningful. Logion 15 ('that one is your Father') is capitalised because the saying identifies the Father with one 'not born of woman', the standard reading in the commentaries.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): capitalised for the divine referent at 40, 44, 50, 57, 61, 64, 69, 76; lower case for human fathers at 53 ('their father'), 55 ('his father') and 72 ('my father's possessions'). v1.2.0 (Block C): capitalised for the divine referent at 79 ('the word of the Father'), 83, 96, 97, 98, 99 ('my Father'), 113; lower case for human fathers at 101 ('his father') and at 105 ('the father and the mother'), where the referent is not established.

entries.source: ⲙⲛ̄ⲧϩⲏⲕⲉ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϩⲏⲕⲉ 'poor' (abstract ⲙⲛ̄ⲧϩⲏⲕⲉ 'poverty'); Greek πτωχεία G4432 (P.Oxy. 654.21, 1.22, partly restored)
entries.literal: poverty
entries.standardEnglish: 'poverty' (all standard translations)
entries.wohChoice: 'poverty' (THOM-3 ×2, THOM-29); the adjective ϩⲏⲕⲉ = 'poor' when it occurs (logion 54, Block B), so the English pair poverty/poor mirrors the Coptic pair.
entries.rationale: ⲙⲛ̄ⲧϩⲏⲕⲉ is the regular abstract noun built on ϩⲏⲕⲉ 'poor', and 'poverty' is its plain English equivalent; the Greek has πτωχεία. 'Destitution' or 'want' would sharpen the tone beyond the Coptic. Using the same English noun in 3 and 29 keeps the collection's contrast between spiritual 'wealth' and 'poverty' visible across sayings.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): ϩⲏⲕⲉ 'the poor' at 54, as anticipated.

entries.source: ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ; ⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ; ⲟⲩⲁ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲟⲩⲁ 'one'; s.v. ⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'single, only'; Greek P.Oxy. 654.27 [ἓν καὶ ταὐτό?] (restored)
entries.literal: one alone / one only
entries.standardEnglish: 'a single one' (Lambdin 4, 23); 'one and the same' (Lambdin 22)
entries.wohChoice: 'a single one' (THOM-4, 23); 'the single one' for ⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ with the demonstrative article (THOM-22); plain 'one' for ⲟⲩⲁ alone (THOM-11 'when you were one'; THOM-22 'make the two one'). Kept distinct from ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ 'solitary' (see that entry).
entries.rationale: ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ is literally 'one single', and 'a single one' keeps both the numeral and the intensifier; 'one and the same' interprets it as identity of the two, which is one reading of logion 22 but not the only one. A single English rendering across 4, 22 and 23 lets the reader see that the three sayings use the same phrase, which is the textual basis for the commentators' discussion of unification in Thomas (Klijn 1962; DeConick 2006; Gathercole 2014). The phrase is kept apart from the Greek loan ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ, because the collection uses both and the relation between them is itself debated.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): adjectival ⲟⲩⲱⲧ without ⲟⲩⲁ = 'single' ('this single house' 48, 'this single pearl' 76); ⲡⲟⲩⲁ … ⲡⲕⲉⲟⲩⲁ 'the one … the other' (47); ⲡⲟⲩⲁ … ⲡⲟⲩⲁ 'one … one' (61). Indefinite ⲟⲩⲁ 'someone' at 61 is governed by `shesh-equal-and-logion-61-crux-thomas-woh`. v1.2.0 (Block C): 'make the two one' (106, as at 22); ⲡⲓⲟⲩⲁ 'the one' and ⲟⲩⲁ ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲟⲩ 'one of them' (107).

entries.source: ⲡⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ ⲙ̄ⲡⲱⲛϩ; ⲡⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ ⲉⲧⲕⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ; ⲡⲙⲁ
entries.strongs: G5117 (τόπος); Crum s.v. ⲙⲁ 'place'; s.v. ⲧⲥⲁⲃⲟ 'teach, show'
entries.literal: the place of life; the place where you are
entries.standardEnglish: 'the place of life' (Lambdin; Meyer); 'Show us the place where you are' (Lambdin); 'Teach us about the place' (other translations)
entries.wohChoice: 'place' for both ⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ (THOM-4, 24) and native ⲙⲁ (THOM-12, 18); 'the place of life' (THOM-4). ⲙⲁⲧⲥⲉⲃⲟⲛ ⲉⲡⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ (THOM-24) = 'Show us the place', ⲧⲥⲁⲃⲟ in its sense 'make known, show'.
entries.rationale: Coptic uses the Greek loan ⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ and the native ⲙⲁ without a clear difference of meaning in these sayings, and English has one natural word for both; the loan/native distinction is recorded here rather than forced into the line (see `greek-loanword-rendering-convention-thomas-woh`). 'The place of life' is the literal rendering and the standard one; 'region' would import a spatial technicality that the Coptic does not require. In 24, ⲧⲥⲁⲃⲟ ⲉ- can mean 'teach about' or 'show, make known'; 'Show us' fits the disciples' request to see where Jesus is and is Lambdin's rendering, with 'teach us about' recorded in commentary.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'place' at 50, 60, 68 (both ⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ and ⲙⲁ), 76; plural ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ 'the places' (64). Not applied where ⲙⲁ forms a compound or idiom: ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ 'the bridal chamber' (75), ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲧⲏⲣϥ 'entirely' (67), ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲉⲗⲟⲟⲗⲉ 'vineyard' (65). v1.2.0 (Block C): ⲙⲁ 'place' (86 '[a] place to lay his head').

entries.source: ⲣⲱⲙⲉ; ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ; ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ; ⲣⲙ̄ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧ; ⲣⲙ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲣⲱⲙⲉ 'man, human being, person' (construct ⲣⲙ̄-); Greek ἄνθρωπος G444
entries.literal: a human being / a man
entries.standardEnglish: 'man' (Lambdin throughout); 'person / human' (Patterson–Meyer in places)
entries.wohChoice: Traditional generic 'man' as the base for singular ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ / ⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ (THOM-4, 7, 8, 21, 24), as in matthew-woh; predicative ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ 'human' where the contrast is species (THOM-7 'the lion will become human'); plural 'people' (THOM-16); fixed phrases 'the heart of man' (THOM-17) and 'the sons of men' (THOM-28); compounds 'wise' (ⲣⲙ̄ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧ, THOM-8, 13), 'a man of light' (ⲣⲙ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ, THOM-24), 'a man of understanding' (THOM-21).
entries.rationale: ⲣⲱⲙⲉ is the generic word for a human being, so the English has to pick a register; the program's NT translations use the traditional generic 'man' (matthew-woh 13:31 'a man took and sowed'), and Thomas follows them so that parallel sayings read alike. Where the saying contrasts human and animal (logion 7, the lion becoming ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ), 'human' states the contrast more exactly than 'man'. The plural is 'people' in 16 because the Coptic generic plural there has no gender focus. No lens is involved; Blocks B and C follow the same mix.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): generic 'man' throughout (45, 47, 57, 58, 63, 64, 65, 76); vocatives 'Who are you, man?' (61) and 'O man' (72); appositive 'a man, a merchant' (76). v1.2.0 (Block C): generic 'man' (78, 83 'to man', 98, 103, 109); appositive 'a man, a shepherd' (107, as 76); 'sons of man' (106); plural ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ 'people' (113). ⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ at 86 is governed by the central Son-of-Man entry.

entries.source: ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉ …
entries.strongs: G3107 (μακάριος); Greek μακάριος (P.Oxy. 654.41, traces)
entries.partOfSpeech: predicate noun in nominal sentence ('a blessed one is …')
entries.literal: a blessed one is the one who …
entries.standardEnglish: 'Blessed is …' (Lambdin; Layton; Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'Blessed is …' (THOM-7, 18, 19), matching matthew-woh's 'Blessed are …'. The central Mt 5:3-12 beatitudes entry is not applied to these three sayings, which are not synoptic beatitudes; the plural synoptic-parallel beatitudes of Thomas (54, 68, 69) are proposed for that entry in Blocks B/C.
entries.rationale: ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲡⲉ is the Coptic singular form of the beatitude formula, and 'Blessed is' is the established English, consistent with the program's rendering of μακάριος in Matthew. The central entry `beatitudes-mt-5-3-12-makarios-formula-ethical-teaching-cross-corpus` documents the Sermon on the Mount beatitudes as a pericope; logia 7, 18 and 19 (the lion, standing at the beginning, existing before coming into being) have no synoptic counterpart, so citing that entry would imply a parallel that does not exist. The lexical decision is the same, and is recorded here; the commentary of 7, 18 and 19 does not discuss the synoptic beatitudes.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): the singular 'Blessed is' at 58; the plural non-synoptic beatitude ϩⲉⲛⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ ⲛⲉ at 49 is 'Blessed are' under this entry. The synoptic-parallel beatitudes 54, 68, 69 cite the central beatitudes entry. v1.2.0 (Block C): '[Blessed] is the man who knows' (103); not a synoptic beatitude, so the central beatitudes entry is not cited. The native beatitude ⲛⲁⲓⲁⲧ= at 79 is also 'Blessed', under `naiat-native-beatitude-blessed-thomas-woh`.

entries.source: ⲁⲩⲱ ⲡⲙⲟⲩⲉⲓ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ; ϥⲃⲏⲧ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲙⲟⲩⲓ 'lion'; s.v. ⲃⲱⲧⲉ 'be abhorrent, polluted' (stative ⲃⲏⲧ)
entries.literal: and the lion will become man; he is abominable
entries.standardEnglish: manuscript reading 'and the lion becomes man' (Lambdin); emendation 'and the man will become lion' (proposed by a number of modern editors and commentators; discussed in Jackson 1985)
entries.wohChoice: Keep the manuscript reading in the line: 'and the lion will become human'; ϥⲃⲏⲧ = 'loathsome'. The emendation and its grounds are given in commentary.
entries.rationale: The second half repeats the outcome of the first ('the lion will become human'), which is why many editors suspect a scribal slip and emend to 'the man will become lion', the result the symmetry seems to require. The manuscript reading is nevertheless grammatical and has been defended as meaningful (Jackson, The Lion Becomes Man, 1985, reads it against a Platonic and gnostic background), and no Greek survives to decide. The program's rule for cruxes (register convention; brief for this text) is to print what the manuscript says and to put conjecture in the apparatus, so the English keeps the transmitted text. 'Loathsome' renders the stative of ⲃⲱⲧⲉ 'be abhorrent'; 'cursed' (Lambdin) is the antithesis the context invites but not the lexical meaning.

entries.literal: Look, the one who sows went out …
entries.standardEnglish: 'Now the sower went out' (Lambdin); 'Look, the sower went out' (Patterson–Meyer); matthew-woh 13:3 'Behold, the sower went out to sow'
entries.wohChoice: 'Behold, the sower went out' (matching matthew-woh's 'Behold' for presentative ἰδού / ⲉⲓⲥϩⲏⲏⲧⲉ, here and at THOM-3, 10); the Coptic soils are kept as Thomas has them: 'the path', 'the rock' (singular), 'the thorns', 'the good soil'; 'the worm ate them'; 'sixty per measure and one hundred twenty per measure'. The central Matthean sower entry is NOT applied: Thomas lacks 'to sow' and the allegorical interpretation, and its soils and yields differ.
entries.rationale: Thomas's sower is a parallel to the synoptic parable, not a copy: it has the singular 'rock', an added worm, ears sent 'toward the sky', and yields of sixty and one hundred and twenty 'per measure', and it has no interpretation (contrast Mt 13:18-23). The shared opening is rendered as in matthew-woh so that the parallel is visible, while the divergent details stay as the Coptic has them, which is the point a reader comparing the versions needs to see. The central `parable-of-the-sower-mt-13-3-23-…` entry governs the Matthean wording and records a Raëlian-canon reading attached to Matthew's text; extending it to Thomas would attach that reception to a text the canon does not cite, so the overlay records the Thomas form separately and only cross-references it.
entries.scopeNote: v1.2.0 (Block C): presentative ⲉⲓⲥϩⲏⲏⲧⲉ 'Behold' (113 'Behold, here … Behold, there'; 114 'Behold, I myself will lead her'). Only the 'Behold' rule of this entry applies; the sower vocabulary does not.

entries.source: ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ; ⲡⲕⲁϩ
entries.strongs: G2889 (κόσμος); Crum s.v. ⲕⲁϩ 'earth, ground, land'
entries.literal: the world; the earth / the ground
entries.standardEnglish: 'the world' for κόσμος; 'the earth', 'the soil', 'the ground' for ⲕⲁϩ (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'the world' for ⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ (THOM-10, 16, 21, 24, 27, 28); 'the earth' for ⲕⲁϩ in cosmic contexts (THOM-12 'heaven and earth', 16 'divisions upon the earth') and 'the soil' / 'any land' in agricultural or geographical ones (THOM-9, 14, 20). THOM-21 ⲣⲟⲉⲓⲥ ϩⲁⲧⲉϩⲏ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ = 'keep watch against the world'.
entries.rationale: Thomas uses the Greek loan ⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ for the human world (to be fasted from, renounced, illuminated) and the native ⲕⲁϩ for the physical earth and soil, and the English pair world/earth keeps that distinction audible. 'Cosmos' or 'world-order' would over-technicalise a loan that is common in Coptic. In logion 21 ϩⲁⲧⲉϩⲏ 'before, in the face of' with the vigilance verb is rendered 'against', which is the sense all standard translations give ('be on guard against the world').
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'on earth' (44, ⲕⲁϩ); 'the new world' (51); 'the world' (56). v1.2.0 (Block C): 'the world' for ⲕⲟⲥⲙⲟⲥ (80, 110, 111); 'the earth' for ⲕⲁϩ (91 'the sky and the earth', 111, 113 'spread out upon the earth').

entries.source: ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ; ⲣ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ; ⲣⲙ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ 'light'; ⲣ̄ ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ 'give light, shine'; Greek φῶς G5457 (P.Oxy. 655 fragment d, traces)
entries.literal: light; make light; man of light
entries.standardEnglish: 'There is light within a man of light, and he (or: it) lights up the whole world' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'light' (THOM-11, 24, 33); ⲣ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ 'give light' (THOM-24); ⲣⲙ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ 'a man of light' (THOM-24). In THOM-24 the subject ϥ- is rendered 'he' (the man of light), with 'it' (the light, masculine ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ) given in commentary.
entries.rationale: ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ is the ordinary word for light, and its compounds are transparent. The only real decision is the subject of ϥⲣ̄ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ in 24: the masculine pronoun can resume either 'a man of light' or 'light', and Lambdin prints both. 'He' keeps the saying about the person whom the disciples asked about ('the place where you are'), and the alternative is stated in commentary so the ambiguity is not hidden.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'the light' (50); 'filled with light' (61). v1.2.0 (Block C): 'I am the light' (77); 'the light that is in them … the light of the Father … his light' (83). In 83 the subject of ϥⲛⲁϭⲱⲗⲡ is rendered 'He' (the Father), with 'it' (the light) in commentary, as at 24.

entries.strongs: G2385 (Ἰάκωβος); G1342 (δίκαιος); Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 2.23 (Hegesippus on 'James the Just'); Layton, Coptic Grammar §§ on the focalising (second) future
entries.partOfSpeech: proper name + epithet; relative and focalising-future clauses
entries.literal: James the righteous; the place you have come to, it is to James that you will go
entries.standardEnglish: 'Wherever you are, you are to go to James the righteous' (Lambdin); 'James the Just' (Patterson–Meyer; the Eusebian tradition)
entries.wohChoice: 'James the Righteous' (ⲇⲓⲕⲁⲓⲟⲥ = 'righteous', as in 'a righteous angel', THOM-13); 'Who is it that will be great over us?'; 'Wherever you have come to, you are to go to James the Righteous' (SURFACE CHANGE from the draft's 'Wherever you have come, you will go').
entries.rationale: The name and epithet are direct: Ἰάκωβος is conventionally 'James' in English, and ⲇⲓⲕⲁⲓⲟⲥ is 'righteous', the same loan the block renders 'righteous' in 13; 'the Just' is the familiar Eusebian English but would break that concordance. The inferred part is the clause: ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛⲁⲃⲱⲕ is the focalising (second) future, which focuses the goal 'to James' and, in a reply to 'who will lead us?', carries a directive sense that Lambdin renders 'you are to go'; the draft's plain 'you will go' loses that. ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲉⲓ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ is 'the place you have come to' (ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ 'there' resumes the place); 'to' is supplied in English to keep the direction, since a reader could otherwise take 'wherever you have come' as 'wherever you have come from'.

entries.translit: p-sah; angelos; philosophos; pēgē et-brbre; šit=
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲥⲁϩ 'teacher, master'; s.v. ⲃⲣ̄ⲃⲣ̄ 'bubble, boil'; s.v. ϣⲓ 'measure'; G32 (ἄγγελος); G5386 (φιλόσοφος); G4077 (πηγή)
entries.lemma: ⲥⲁϩ; ⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ; ⲫⲓⲗⲟⲥⲟⲫⲟⲥ; ⲡⲏⲅⲏ; ⲃⲣ̄ⲃⲣ̄; ϣⲓ
entries.literal: teacher; a righteous angel; a philosopher-man of wisdom; the bubbling spring which I measured
entries.standardEnglish: 'Master' (Lambdin); 'Teacher' (Patterson–Meyer); 'a righteous angel', 'a wise philosopher', 'the bubbling spring which I have measured out' (Lambdin); 'which I have tended' (Patterson–Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'Teacher' (and 'I am not your teacher'); 'a righteous angel'; 'a wise philosopher'; 'my mouth is wholly unable to say'; 'the bubbling spring that I have measured out'.
entries.rationale: ⲥⲁϩ is the ordinary Coptic word for 'teacher', and using 'Teacher' in both Thomas's address and Jesus's reply keeps the point of the exchange (Jesus refuses the title Thomas has just used). ⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ is rendered 'angel' because the comparison is with a heavenly being of the Hellenistic-Jewish type, as in the program's renderings of Greek ἄγγελος in 1 Enoch and Jubilees; the program's Hebrew convention 'messenger' for malʾāḵ is not carried into this Greek loan, and the ambiguity is noted in commentary. ϣⲓ is 'measure', so 'measured out' is literal; 'tended' is an interpretive paraphrase that the lexicon does not support directly. ⲛⲁϣϣⲁⲡϥ ⲁⲛ (with the editorial ⟨ϣ⟩) is 'is unable / does not allow', and 'wholly unable' renders ϩⲟⲗⲱⲥ with it.

entries.source: ⲡⲛ︤ⲁ︥ (ⲡⲛⲉⲩⲙⲁ); ⲥⲁⲣⲝ; ⲥⲱⲙⲁ; ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ
entries.strongs: G4151 (πνεῦμα); G4561 (σάρξ); G4983 (σῶμα); Crum s.v. ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ 'wonder'
entries.literal: spirit; flesh; body; wonder
entries.standardEnglish: 'spirit', 'flesh', 'body', 'a wonder … a wonder of wonders' (Lambdin; all standard translations)
entries.wohChoice: 'spirit' in lower case (THOM-14 'your spirits', THOM-29); 'flesh' for ⲥⲁⲣⲝ and 'body' for ⲥⲱⲙⲁ, kept distinct (THOM-28, 29); ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ 'wonder', with ⲣ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ 'marvel' (THOM-2, 29).
entries.rationale: In 14 the plural 'your spirits' shows that ⲡⲛⲉⲩⲙⲁ is the human spirit, and in 29 the flesh/spirit/body argument is about the relation of spirit to body, not about the Holy Spirit (which Thomas names as such at logion 44), so capitalisation would mislead. ⲥⲁⲣⲝ and ⲥⲱⲙⲁ are distinct Greek loans and the saying turns on them, so they are not merged. The ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ / ⲣ̄ϣⲡⲏⲣⲉ pair links logion 29's 'wonder' to logion 2's 'he will marvel', and the English keeps the shared root visible. 'Breath' for ⲡⲛⲉⲩⲙⲁ is not adopted: the program's central breath readings belong to Hebrew rûaḥ, and Thomas's Greek loan here contrasts with body.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'the Holy Spirit' (44, as anticipated, under `son-and-holy-spirit-triad-logion-44-thomas-woh`); lower-case 'in spirit' (53). v1.2.0 (Block C): 'the body' for ⲥⲱⲙⲁ (80, against 'corpse' for ⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ at 56; 87); 'the flesh' (112); 'a living spirit' lower case (114).

entries.source: ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩϫⲡⲟϥ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲥϩⲓⲙⲉ; ⲡⲉϩⲧ ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ϩⲟ
entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϫⲡⲟ 'beget, bear'; s.v. ⲡⲁϩⲧ 'bow down, prostrate'
entries.literal: the one whom they did not beget from the woman
entries.standardEnglish: 'one who was not born of woman' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'one who was not born of woman'; 'prostrate yourselves on your faces and worship him'.
entries.rationale: The Coptic uses an impersonal active ('whom they did not beget'), which English renders naturally as a passive, as all standard translations do. 'Of woman' without the article follows the idiom of Job 14:1 and Mt 11:11 ('born of women'), which is the intertext an English reader recognises; the Coptic article is generic. ⲡⲉϩⲧ ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄ ⲉϫⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ϩⲟ is the full prostration formula and is rendered literally.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): ϫⲡⲟ by context: 'those born of women' (46); 'beget' of a human father (53); 'bring forth' of what is produced from within (70).

entries.source: ⲉⲩⲟ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ
entries.strongs: LSJ s.v. μοναχός 'single, solitary'; not in the NT; Judge, 'The Earliest Use of Monachos for Monk', JbAC 20 (1977)
entries.literal: being monachoi (single / solitary ones)
entries.standardEnglish: 'they will stand solitary' (Lambdin); 'they will stand alone' (Patterson–Meyer); 'solitaries' or 'single ones' in other translations
entries.wohChoice: 'they will stand as solitary ones' (THOM-16; also logia 49 and 75 in Blocks B/C). Not transliterated; not rendered 'monks'; kept distinct from ⲟⲩⲁ ⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'a single one'.
entries.rationale: μοναχός means 'single, solitary', and in the fourth century it becomes the standard word for 'monk'; Thomas is among the earliest Christian texts to use it, and what it means here (unmarried, singular in the sense of undivided, or separated from family, which fits the household strife of 16) is debated (Klijn 1962; DeConick 2006; Gathercole 2014). 'Solitary ones' keeps the literal sense without choosing between those readings and without the anachronism 'monks'. Because the rendering takes a position within a live debate (against 'single ones' or 'unified ones'), it is `inferred`, and the alternatives are given in commentary.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'the solitary and chosen ones' (49, word order adjusted for the relative ⲉⲧⲥⲟⲧⲡ); 'the solitary ones' (75).

entries.source: ⲧⲁⲣⲭⲏ; ⲑⲁⲏ (ⲧ-ϩⲁⲏ)
entries.strongs: G746 (ἀρχή); Crum s.v. ϩⲁⲏ 'end, last'
entries.literal: the beginning; the end
entries.standardEnglish: 'the beginning … the end' (Lambdin; Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'the beginning' / 'the end'; 'Blessed is the one who will stand at the beginning'.
entries.rationale: ἀρχή can mean 'beginning', 'origin' or 'first principle', but in a saying that pairs it with ϩⲁⲏ 'end' and answers a question about 'our end', the temporal pair beginning/end is the sense the context requires and the one all standard translations give. 'Origin' or 'source' would introduce a metaphysical reading that the saying may imply but does not state. The rasura in ⲥⲟⲩⲱⲛⲑϩⲁⲏ (a deleted ϩ) does not affect the reading and is recorded in commentary.

entries.source: ϯⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲛ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲇⲓⲥⲟⲥ ⲉⲥⲉⲕⲓⲙ ⲁⲛ ⲛ̄ϣⲱⲙ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲱ
entries.strongs: G3857 (παράδεισος); Crum s.v. ϣⲏⲛ 'tree'; s.v. ⲕⲓⲙ 'move'; s.v. ϣⲱⲙ 'summer'; s.v. ⲡⲣⲱ 'winter'
entries.literal: five trees in paradise, which do not move summer (or) winter
entries.standardEnglish: 'five trees for you in Paradise which remain undisturbed summer and winter' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'five trees in Paradise that do not move in summer or in winter, and their leaves do not fall'; 'Paradise' capitalised, without article, as the proper name of the garden.
entries.rationale: ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲇⲓⲥⲟⲥ is the Septuagint word for the garden of Eden (Gen 2:8), and the capitalised 'Paradise' without article is the English convention for that place; 'the garden' would lose the Greek term the Coptic keeps. The relative clause is rendered literally ('do not move'), with the seasons supplied with 'in' as English requires. The number five has no parallel in Genesis; its later appearance in Coptic gnostic and Manichaean texts and the readings it has received are recorded in commentary, not in the line.

entries.source: ⲙⲁⲣⲓϩⲁⲙ
entries.strongs: G3137 (Μαριάμ / Μαρία); Hebrew Miryām
entries.literal: Mariham
entries.standardEnglish: 'Mary' (Lambdin; Patterson–Meyer); 'Mariam' / 'Mariham' (some editions keep the form)
entries.wohChoice: 'Mariham' (the manuscript's spelling, here and at logion 114). The text does not say which Mary; the usual identification with Mary Magdalene is given in commentary.
entries.rationale: ⲙⲁⲣⲓϩⲁⲙ is the Coptic spelling of Mariam (with an orthographic ϩ), a form also found in other Coptic texts, and keeping it lets the reader see that Thomas does not say 'Mary Magdalene' or 'Mary the mother'. Normalising to 'Mary' would make the English look as specific as the canonical gospels, which usually add an identifier. The identification with Mary Magdalene is the majority view in the commentaries, on the basis of logion 114 and other second- and third-century texts in which a Mariam questions Jesus, and is recorded as such in commentary.
entries.scopeNote: v1.2.0 (Block C): 'Mariham' at 114, as anticipated.

entries.source: ϣⲓⲛⲁ ϫⲉⲛⲉⲛ̄ⲗⲏⲥⲧⲏⲥ ϩⲉ ⲉϩⲓⲏ ⲉⲉⲓ ϣⲁⲣⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲉⲡⲉⲓ ⲧⲉⲭⲣⲉⲓⲁ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ϭⲱϣⲧ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲏⲧⲥ ⲥⲉⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲟⲥ
entries.translit: šina je ne-n-lēstēs he e-hiē; tekhreia
entries.strongs: G3027 (λῃστής); G5532 (χρεία); Layton, Coptic Grammar (negative optative ⲛ̄ⲛⲉ-)
entries.lemma: ⲗⲏⲥⲧⲏⲥ; ϩⲉ ⲉ-; ⲭⲣⲉⲓⲁ; ϭⲱϣⲧ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ
entries.literal: so that the robbers [not?] find a way to come to you, since the need you are looking out for, they will find it
entries.standardEnglish: 'lest the robbers find a way to come to you, for the difficulty which you expect will (surely) materialize' (Lambdin); 'so that the robbers can't find a way to get to you, for the trouble you expect will come' (Patterson–Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'so that the robbers do not find a way to come to you, for the need you are watching out for, they will find it' (SURFACE CHANGE: 'it' added for the object pronoun of ⲉⲣⲟⲥ, which the draft omitted). The negative sense is printed without brackets; the reading of ⲛⲉ as the negative optative ⲛ̄ⲛⲉ is explained in commentary.
entries.rationale: As written, ⲛⲉ- before ⲛ̄ⲗⲏⲥⲧⲏⲥ is tagged by the corpus as a preterite converter, which gives no negation and no coherent clause; every standard translation reads the clause as negative purpose ('lest the robbers find'), which requires taking ⲛⲉ as a spelling of the negative optative ⲛ̄ⲛⲉ- (or emending to it). The context (gird yourselves so that robbers do not get in) makes the negative sense certain, so the English prints it without brackets, but the reading is still an editorial inference and is labelled `inferred`. In the following clause ⲥⲉⲛⲁϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲟⲥ has an explicit object ('they will find it', it = ⲧⲉⲭⲣⲉⲓⲁ), and the English now renders it; Lambdin and Patterson–Meyer paraphrase the clause idiomatically ('the difficulty you expect will materialize'), and that sense is given in commentary rather than adopted, so that the English stays close to the Coptic syntax.

entries.source: ⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ ⲉⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ
entries.strongs: G1504 (εἰκών)
entries.literal: an image in the place of an image
entries.standardEnglish: 'a likeness in place of a likeness' (Lambdin); 'an image in place of an image' (Patterson–Meyer)
entries.wohChoice: 'an image in place of an image' (THOM-22); 'image(s)' at its later occurrences (logia 50, 83, 84). ⲉⲩϫⲓⲉⲣⲱⲧⲉ = 'being nursed'.
entries.rationale: εἰκών is 'image', and the same English at every occurrence lets readers connect logion 22 with the cluster of image sayings in 83-84, where Thomas speaks of the images of humans and the image of the Father. 'Likeness' would blur the distinction between εἰκών and ὁμοίωσις that the Genesis background (Gen 1:26 LXX κατ᾽ εἰκόνα … καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν) keeps. ϫⲓ ⲉⲣⲱⲧⲉ is 'take milk', so 'being nursed' is literal.
entries.scopeNote: v1.1.0 (Block B): 'in their image' (50), referent of 'their' left unresolved. v1.2.0 (Block C): 'the images … the image of the light … his image' (83); 'your images' (84), kept distinct from native ⲉⲓⲛⲉ 'likeness' (84).

entries.source: ⲯⲩⲭⲏ (ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲕⲯⲩⲭⲏ; ⲁⲧⲁⲯⲩⲭⲏ ϯⲧⲕⲁⲥ)
entries.strongs: G5590 (ψυχή)
entries.literal: soul / self / life
entries.standardEnglish: 'Love your brother like your soul' (Lambdin); 'my soul was afflicted' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'soul' at both occurrences: 'Love your brother as your soul' (THOM-25); 'my soul was pained' (THOM-28).
entries.rationale: ψυχή covers 'life', 'self' and 'soul', and in 25 the idiom stands behind Lev 19:18 'as yourself' (Hebrew kāmôkā; in Semitic idiom nepeš is often the self). Rendering 'as yourself' would harmonise Thomas with the synoptic love command, which the convention forbids; 'as your soul' keeps the Coptic noun and the standard rendering, and the reflexive sense is explained in commentary. A single rendering at both occurrences lets the reader see that the collection uses the same word for the self that loves and for the self of Jesus that grieves.

entries.literal: in your ear, in the other ear; under a measure
entries.standardEnglish: 'Preach from your housetops that which you will hear in your ear (and) in the other ear' (Lambdin); 'under a bushel' (Lambdin); 'under a basket' (Patterson–Meyer; matthew-woh 5:15 for μόδιος)
entries.wohChoice: Keep the manuscript sequence: 'What you will hear in your ear, in the other ear proclaim it upon your rooftops'. ϩⲁⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ = 'under a measure' (SURFACE CHANGE from the draft's 'basket'), so that the Coptic wordplay ear/measure stays within reach of the commentary.
entries.rationale: 'In the other ear' may be a dittography of 'in your ear' or may mean 'into another's ear'; the Greek ('in your one ear') supports a two-ear contrast and therefore a meaningful text, so the English keeps the manuscript sequence and records both readings in commentary. ⲙⲁⲁϫⲉ is both 'ear' and a dry 'measure', and Thomas uses it in both senses within one saying; Mt 5:15's μόδιος is likewise a measure, which 'basket' (matthew-woh) and 'bushel' (KJV, Lambdin) paraphrase. 'Measure' is the literal sense of the Coptic noun and is the only English that lets the commentary point to the pun; the departure from matthew-woh's 'basket' is a deliberate difference between two source texts and is `inferred` because it rests on reading the pun as intended.

entries.source: Thomas 3 (ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ ⲥⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ϩⲟⲩⲛ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲥⲙ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲃⲁⲗ); 18 (ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲁⲣⲭⲏ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ ⲉⲑⲁϩⲏ ⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ); 19 (ϯⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ϣⲏⲛ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲇⲓⲥⲟⲥ)
entries.partOfSpeech: interpretive reading recorded in the apparatus (no effect on the English)
entries.literal: the kingdom is inside you and outside you; where the beginning is, there the end will be; five trees in Paradise
entries.standardEnglish: Mainstream readings: 3 as a critique of apocalyptic localisation and a call to self-knowledge; 18 as a return to the primordial state (protology as eschatology); 19 as a symbol of unchanging life in Paradise, variously allegorised
entries.wohChoice: No effect on any English line. The entry records, as an interpretive reading, three resonances a Wheel of Heaven reader will notice: (3) self-knowledge as recognising oneself as a child of ‘the living Father’, read alongside the canon's teaching that humans were made in the image of the Elohim; (18) the identity of beginning and end, read alongside the cyclical precessional framework from which the project takes its name; (19) the five unchanging trees of Paradise, read alongside the canon's reading of the Eden of Genesis 2 as the Elohim's place of work. Each appears once, in a commentary paragraph labelled 'Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation)'.
entries.rationale: None of the three sayings refers to the Elohim, to precessional ages or to a physical garden of the creators; the resonances are an interpretive synthesis that goes beyond what Thomas or any single source states, which is the definition of `speculative`. Logion 3 in fact mocks the idea that the kingdom is located 'in the sky', so the commentary states that it gives no support to a reading of the kingdom as a place in the sky. The entry exists so that every point at which the lens touches the Thomas apparatus is listed in one auditable place and can be removed with one decision: if the reviewer declines it, delete the labelled paragraph from the notes of THOM-3, 18 and 19 and drop this id from their glossaryRefs; nothing else depends on it. Ratified at human sign-off on 2026-11-01 (zarazinsfuss), apparatus only.

entries.source: ⟨ⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩ⟩ (THOM-60) in the Dilley edition; English ⟨ ⟩
entries.partOfSpeech: editorial convention (refines rule 2 of the restored-text convention)
entries.literal: a whole word supplied by the modern editor where the manuscript has none
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin prints '<They saw> a Samaritan'; other translations supply the verb silently
entries.wohChoice: Rule 2 of `restored-text-bracket-and-sigla-convention-thomas-woh` (⟨ ⟩ and ( ) rendered silently) is limited to supplied letters: scribal slips and abbreviations inside a word the scribe did write. Where the source's ⟨ ⟩ supplies a whole word that the manuscript does not contain, the English word(s) for it stand in English angle brackets ⟨ ⟩, the form the Block A convention reserves for wording with no manuscript basis. Block B has one case: '⟨They saw⟩ a Samaritan' (THOM-60).
entries.rationale: Block A's rule 2 rests on the argument that bracketing a whole English word for a one-letter slip would make the text look damaged when it is not; that argument does not hold when the supplied item is itself a whole word, because then a silent rendering tells the reader that the manuscript contains a verb it does not contain. At THOM-60 the manuscript begins ⲁⲩⲥⲁⲙⲁⲣⲉⲓⲧⲏⲥ with no main verb, and Dilley's ⟨ⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩ⟩ 'they saw' is a modern supply (made likely by the preposition ⲁ- = ⲉ- that ⲛⲁⲩ ⲉ- 'see' governs, and by a possible haplography of ⲁⲩ), so the English marks it exactly as the reserved ⟨ ⟩ is defined. The rule stays mechanical and auditable: letters are silent, whole words are marked. It does not license supplying speech formulas the Coptic lacks (see the register convention and THOM-43, THOM-61).
entries.scopeNote: Ratified at sign-off (2026-11-01): THOM-61 '⟨Salome said:⟩' — the Coptic has no speech formula, but the feminine possessive ⲧⲉⲕ- marks Salome as the speaker of 'I am your disciple'; admitted as a narrow exception for a speaker the grammar identifies, not as a licence to supply speech formulas generally.

entries.partOfSpeech: Greek loan noun; native noun; verb
entries.literal: the keys of the knowledge; they hid them
entries.standardEnglish: 'the keys of knowledge' (Lambdin, with '(gnosis)' added in parentheses); Lk 11:52 'the key of knowledge'
entries.wohChoice: 'the keys of knowledge', and 'have hidden them' for active ϩⲱⲡ (the verb whose stative gives 'hidden' in the incipit). ⲅⲛⲱⲥⲓⲥ is translated, not transliterated; its only occurrence in Thomas is THOM-39.
entries.rationale: γνῶσις means 'knowledge', and the loanword convention requires a translation; 'knowledge' is also the word of the Lukan parallel (Lk 11:52) in the standard English versions, so the saying stays recognisable. Transliterating 'gnosis' would turn a single occurrence of an ordinary Greek loan into a technical term and pre-judge the debated question of Thomas's relation to later 'gnostic' systems, which the apparatus states without deciding (THOM-0). The plural 'keys' follows the Coptic, where the resumptive object of ⲁⲩϩⲟⲡⲟⲩ is plural, against Luke's singular; ϩⲱⲡ is rendered with the same English root as the stative ϩⲏⲡ of the incipit so that the link between 'hidden sayings' and 'hidden keys' remains visible.

entries.literal: become, you passing by
entries.standardEnglish: 'Become passers-by' (Lambdin); 'Be passersby'; an adverbial reading 'come into being as you pass away' is also argued
entries.wohChoice: 'Become passers-by.' ϣⲱⲡⲉ 'become' keeps its inchoative sense; the circumstantial is read predicatively.
entries.rationale: ϣⲱⲡⲉ + circumstantial is the regular Coptic way of expressing 'become (something)', so the predicative reading is the grammatically simplest, and it is the rendering of the standard English translation (Lambdin). παράγειν means 'pass by' and also 'pass away' (1 Cor 7:31, of the form of this world), so the saying is ambiguous between a call to transience and a call to itinerancy; 'passers-by' keeps both senses open without choosing. The alternative readings are given in the commentary rather than in the line, under the crux rule.

entries.rationale: Ἰουδαῖος is rendered 'Jew' in the standard English translations of Thomas and of the NT, and the program's NT translations follow that usage. entries.standardEnglish: 'the Father … the Son … the Holy Spirit' (standard); Mt 12:32 has 'the Son of Man'
entries.wohChoice: 'the Father', 'the Son', 'the Holy Spirit', capitalised as a triad; the impersonal ⲥⲉⲛⲁⲕⲱ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛⲁϥ is rendered by the passive 'he will be forgiven', as Block A renders impersonal plurals.

entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin varies 'slave' / 'servant'; 'lord' / 'master' by context
entries.wohChoice: ϩⲙϩⲁⲗ = 'slave' at every occurrence (47, 64, 65). ϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ = 'master' where a slave's owner is meant (47 'two masters', 64 'my master', 65 'his master', 'the master'); 'the lord' in lower case at 73, where the Coptic does not say whose lord; the vocative ⲡϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ at 74 is 'Lord', with the capital only because it opens the quoted address.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲥⲱⲧⲡ 'choose' (stative ⲥⲟⲧⲡ 'chosen'); cf. G1588 (ἐκλεκτός)
entries.literal: the solitary ones and who are chosen; we are the chosen of the living Father
entries.standardEnglish: 'the solitary and elect' (Lambdin); 'the elect of the living father' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'chosen' (not 'elect') at 49 and 50, in concordance with the verb ⲥⲱⲧⲡ 'choose' at THOM-8 ('he chose the large fish') and THOM-23 ('I will choose you'). At 49 the relative ⲉⲧⲥⲟⲧⲡ has no article of its own and qualifies ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ, so the line reads 'the solitary and chosen ones' (one group), changed from the draft's 'the solitary ones and the chosen'.
entries.rationale: A Coptic relative clause introduced by bare ⲉⲧ- needs an antecedent, and the only one available at 49 is ⲛ̄ⲙⲟⲛⲁⲭⲟⲥ; a second, separate group would require the article (ⲛⲉⲧⲥⲟⲧⲡ), so the grammar makes the blessed one group, as Lambdin's 'the solitary and elect' also takes it. 'Chosen' is the plain English of ⲥⲱⲧⲡ and keeps the reader able to connect 49 and 50 with the choosing of 8 and 23; 'elect' is accurate but carries a later doctrinal register that the Coptic verb does not. The monachos rendering 'solitary ones' is kept, adjusted to 'the solitary and chosen ones' by English word order only.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲱϩⲉ (ⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧ= 'stand'); s.v. ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ 'appear'; s.v. ⲙⲁⲉⲓⲛ 'sign'; G1504 (εἰκών)
entries.literal: it stood and appeared in their image; is it you?; we are its sons; the sign
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin: 'the light came into being on its own accord and established [itself] and became manifest through their image'; 'Is it you?'; 'We are its children'
entries.wohChoice: 'the place where the light came into being by itself. It [stood] and [appeared] in their image.' The subject of ⲁϥ- is the light ('It'); ⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧ= = 'stood' (literal); ϩⲛ̄ = 'in'; 'their' is left without a stated referent, as in the Coptic. ϫⲉⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲡⲉ = 'Is it you?'. ⲁⲛⲟⲛ ⲛⲉϥϣⲏⲣⲉ = 'We are its sons' (the light as antecedent; 'sons' per the ratified filial rule). ⲡⲙⲁⲉⲓⲛ = 'the sign'.
entries.rationale: The masculine resumptive ϥ- has ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ 'light' (masculine) as its nearest antecedent, and reading 'It' keeps the cosmogonic sequence of the saying (the light comes into being, stands, appears), which is how Lambdin also takes it. ⲱϩⲉ ⲉⲣⲁⲧ= is the ordinary Coptic for 'stand (up)', so 'stood' is the literal rendering of the restored verb, where 'established itself' interprets; both English verbs are bracketed because their Coptic tokens are partly restored, following the mechanical bracket rule even for the single restored letter of ⲉ[ⲃ]ⲟⲗ. The plural possessive of ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ (normalised ⲧⲉⲩ-) has no expressed antecedent, so the English keeps 'their' without resolving it, and any interpretation of it is confined to the commentary.

entries.source: Thomas 50 (ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲛⲉⲓ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲛⲧⲁⲡⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲛ ϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ … ⲁϥⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉ[ⲃ]ⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ)
entries.partOfSpeech: interpretive reading recorded in the apparatus (no effect on the English)
entries.literal: we came from the light, the place where the light came into being by itself; it stood and appeared in their image
entries.standardEnglish: Mainstream readings: a catechism of the soul's origin and return (compare logion 49), with 'the light' as the realm of origin of the elect; the referent of 'their image' is disputed
entries.wohChoice: No effect on any English line. The entry records one interpretive resonance a Wheel of Heaven reader will notice: the saying answers a question of origin ('From where did you come into being?') with a place, and says that the light 'appeared in their image', with a plural possessive the text does not resolve; this can be read alongside 'Let us make man in our image' (Gen 1:26) and the canon's teaching that humans were made in the image of the Elohim. It appears once, in a commentary paragraph of THOM-50 labelled 'Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation)'.
entries.rationale: Logion 50 names no makers, no planet and no place in the sky, and the canon does not cite it; reading the plural 'their' as the Elohim is an interpretive synthesis that goes beyond what Thomas or any single source states, which is the definition of `speculative`. The English line deliberately keeps 'their' unresolved and 'the light' as written, so the lens cannot be read off the translation, and the commentary states the mainstream reading first. The entry exists so that the single point at which the lens touches Block B is listed in one auditable place and can be removed with one decision: if the reviewer declines it, delete the labelled paragraph from the notes of THOM-50 and drop this id from its glossaryRefs; nothing else depends on it. Mainstream commentators already relate logion 50 to Genesis 1 (e.g. DeConick 2006); only reading the unresolved 'their' as the Elohim is speculative. Ratified at human sign-off on 2026-11-01 (zarazinsfuss), apparatus only.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ 'break'; s.v. ϫⲓⲥⲉ 'be high, exalt'; s.v. ⲕⲟⲩⲓ 'small'
entries.partOfSpeech: negative optative; stative of ϫⲓⲥⲉ (substantivised); circumstantial with predicate ⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ
entries.literal: so that his eyes will not be broken; who is higher; being little; he will be high
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin: 'so superior to John the Baptist that his eyes should not be lowered (before him)'
entries.wohChoice: 'so that his eyes should not be lowered' (negative supplied by the normalised layer, printed without brackets; 'lowered' for literal 'broken'); 'more exalted' for ϫⲟⲥⲉ / ϫⲓⲥⲉ; 'becomes a little one' for ⲉϥⲟ ⲛ̄ⲕⲟⲩⲉⲓ.
entries.rationale: ⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ means 'break', and 'his eyes will (not) be broken' has no clear sense in English; 'lowered' (Lambdin) takes it as an idiom for averting or casting down the eyes before a superior, which fits the comparison with John but is an interpretation, hence `inferred`, with the literal sense stated in the commentary. The negative is not written in the diplomatic text: the corpus normalises ϫⲉⲛⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ to the negative optative ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲩⲟⲩⲱϭⲡ, and under the restored-text convention the English follows the normalised reading, as all standard translations do and as Block A did at THOM-21. 'A little one' keeps the link with 'little ones' at THOM-22 and with Mt 11:11 / Lk 7:28 ('the least in the kingdom').

entries.literal: a corpse, a carcass
entries.standardEnglish: 'corpse' (Lambdin at 56); 'carcass' at 60 in some translations
entries.wohChoice: 'corpse' at every occurrence (56, 60 twice), kept distinct from 'body' for ⲥⲱⲙⲁ (THOM-29; the doublet at THOM-80 reads ⲥⲱⲙⲁ).
entries.rationale: πτῶμα means 'fallen thing, corpse, carcass', and 'corpse' fits both the human application of 56 and the slaughtered lamb of 60, so one English word shows that 60 develops 56. The doublet at logion 80 replaces ⲡⲧⲱⲙⲁ with ⲥⲱⲙⲁ 'body', which `pneuma-sarx-soma-spirit-flesh-body-thomas-woh` renders 'body'; keeping the two words apart lets the reader see the variation between the doublets instead of having the translation erase it. 'Carcass' would sound right for the lamb but would break the link with 56.
entries.scopeNote: v1.2.0 (Block C): cited at 80 for the contrast only: the doublet there has ⲥⲱⲙⲁ, rendered 'the body', so the English keeps 'a corpse' (56) and 'the body' (80) apart.

entries.strongs: G2215 (ζιζάνιον); Crum s.v. ϭⲣⲟϭ 'seed', ϩⲱⲗⲉ 'pull up', ⲣⲱⲕϩ 'burn'
entries.literal: darnel; good seed; that we will pull up; they pull them up and burn them
entries.standardEnglish: 'weeds' (Lambdin); 'darnel' / 'tares' / 'weeds' in NT versions
entries.wohChoice: 'darnel' (as matthew-woh 13:25-30); 'in order to pull up' for the quoted first-person intention ϫⲉⲉⲛⲁϩⲱⲗⲉ; the impersonal plural ⲥⲉϩⲟⲗⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉⲣⲟⲕϩⲟⲩ rendered by the passive 'they will be pulled up and burned'.
entries.rationale: ζιζάνιον is the darnel grass (Lolium temulentum) that looks like wheat until it heads, and matthew-woh renders the same word 'darnel' in the parallel parable, so the program's two versions of the parable use one term. ϫⲉ with the first-person-plural future (Dilley: 'Optative/Second Future') is literally 'saying, "We will pull up"', a quoted intention that English expresses as purpose; the literal form is given in the commentary. The impersonal plural is rendered as a passive, as elsewhere in Thomas, and Dilley's suggestion of a conjunctive ⲛ̄ⲥⲉ is noted without changing the sense.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϩⲓⲥⲉ 'labour, be weary, suffer'; cf. Jas 1:12; 1 Pet 3:14
entries.literal: the man who has toiled / suffered
entries.standardEnglish: 'who has suffered' (Lambdin); 'who has toiled' (other translations)
entries.wohChoice: 'the man who has suffered'; the sense 'toil' is given in the commentary. ϩⲓⲥⲉ as a noun at THOM-8 remains 'without difficulty'.
entries.rationale: ϩⲓⲥⲉ covers physical labour, weariness and suffering, so both standard renderings are lexically exact. 'Suffered' follows the beatitude form of the saying, which closely resembles the blessing of the one who endures trial in Jas 1:12 and the one who suffers in 1 Pet 3:14, and it is the reading of the standard English translation. The alternative is recorded in the commentary so that the reader can see that the Coptic word is broader than the English.
entries.scopeNote: v1.2.0 (Block C): noun ϩⲓⲥⲉ 'any trouble' (97); verb ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲣⲉϥϩⲓⲥⲉ 'Having toiled' (107). The word is rendered by context; its range is recorded here.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϭⲱϣⲧ 'look'
entries.literal: look after; look out for
entries.standardEnglish: 'Take heed of the living one' / 'Look to the living one'
entries.wohChoice: 'Look to' for ϭⲱϣⲧ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁ- (59); 'watching out for' for ϭⲱϣⲧ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲏⲧ= (51, as at THOM-21).
entries.rationale: ϭⲱϣⲧ is the ordinary verb 'look', and its sense is set by the preposition: with ⲛ̄ⲥⲁ- 'after' it means to look after or toward something, with ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲏⲧ= to watch out for what is expected. 'Look to the living one' keeps the visual verb that the rest of 59 develops ('seek to see him and be unable to see'), which 'take heed' would lose. 'Watching out for' at 51 repeats the Block A rendering of the same construction at THOM-21, so the reader can connect the two sayings.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲕⲱⲧⲉ 'turn, go round' (ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲱⲧⲉ ⲙ̄- 'around'); G5117 (τόπος)
entries.partOfSpeech: prepositional phrase in a nominal sentence; imperative
entries.literal: that (one) is around the lamb; seek for yourselves a place within a repose
entries.standardEnglish: Translations often supply words: '(Why does) that man (carry) the lamb around?'
entries.wohChoice: Manuscript reading kept: 'That one is around the lamb.' No words are supplied. 'seek a place for yourselves within repose'.
entries.rationale: ⲡⲏ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲱⲧⲉ ⲙ̄- is a complete Coptic nominal sentence ('that one is around …'), so the line can be printed as written, and the crux rule requires the manuscript reading where the difficulty is one of sense rather than grammar. The usual supplements turn the remark into a question about why the man carries the lamb, which fits the disciples' answer but adds words the manuscript does not have; they are given in the commentary. The final instruction uses τόπος and ἀνάπαυσις, rendered 'place' and 'repose' under their entries.

entries.source: ⲥⲁⲗⲱⲙⲏ; ⲁⲛⲟⲕ ⲧⲉⲕⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ
entries.strongs: Mk 15:40; 16:1 (Σαλώμη); Crum s.v. ⲡⲉⲕ- (feminine ⲧⲉⲕ-)
entries.literal: Salome; I am your (female) disciple
entries.standardEnglish: 'Salome'; Lambdin supplies a speech formula before 'I am your disciple'
entries.wohChoice: 'Salome', without further identification in the line. Her reply 'I am your disciple' carries no speech formula in the Coptic, and none is supplied in the English (register convention); the feminine ⲧⲉⲕ-, which identifies the speaker as Salome, is explained in the commentary.
entries.rationale: The name is spelled as in the Greek NT (Σαλώμη, Mk 15:40; 16:1), where a Salome is among the women at the cross and the tomb; Thomas does not say which Salome is meant, so the identification belongs in the commentary. In Coptic the possessive article ⲧⲉⲕ- is feminine and shows that the speaker of 'I am your disciple' is a woman, i.e. Salome; English cannot mark this in the pronoun, and the binding register convention forbids supplying a formula the Coptic lacks. The commentary therefore states the speaker explicitly, and the question whether an English ⟨Salome said:⟩ should be admitted is escalated for human review.
