entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϣⲱϣ 'be equal, level' (stative ϣⲏϣ); s.v. ϣⲱϥ 'be desolate, destroyed' (stative ϣⲏϥ); s.v. ⲡⲱϣ 'divide' (stative ⲡⲏϣ); s.v. ⲟⲩⲁ 'one, someone'
entries.partOfSpeech: relative statives; circumstantial statives; indefinite pronoun
entries.literal: as from someone; the one who exists from the one who is equal; when he is destroyed … when he is divided
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin: 'I am he who exists from the undivided'; emendation ϣⲏϣ for ϣⲏϥ (Layton 1989, p. 74, cited by Dilley)
entries.wohChoice: 'As though from someone' (indefinite ⲟⲩⲁ); 'the one who is equal' for ⲡⲉⲧϣⲏϣ (literal stative); manuscript ϣⲏϥ kept as 'When he is destroyed', 'divided' for ⲡⲏϣ.
entries.rationale: ϣⲏϣ is the stative of ϣⲱϣ 'be equal, level', so 'the one who is equal' is the literal meaning; Lambdin's 'the undivided' interprets it by contrast with ⲡⲏϣ 'divided' later in the saying, and that interpretation is given in the commentary. The manuscript's ϣⲏϥ (stative of ϣⲱϥ 'be desolate, destroyed') may be a slip for ϣⲏϣ, and Dilley's notes record both the suspicion of corruption and the conjectural emendation (Layton 1989, p. 74); the crux rule keeps the manuscript reading in the line and the emendation in the commentary. ⲟⲩⲁ without article is regularly the indefinite 'someone', which gives Salome's challenge a coherent sense (a stranger sharing her couch as if he were someone's guest); 'the One' would read a title into the indefinite pronoun.

entries.strongs: G3466 (μυστήριον); Crum s.v. ϣⲁ (ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ 'be worthy')
entries.literal: it is to those worthy of my mysteries that I tell my mysteries
entries.standardEnglish: 'mysteries' (standard); 'secrets' in some translations
entries.wohChoice: 'mysteries'. The focalising (second) present ⲉⲓ̈ϫⲱ is rendered as a cleft: 'It is to [those who are worthy] of [my] mysteries that I tell my mysteries.' (changed from the draft's uncleft order).
entries.rationale: μυστήριον is the word of Mk 4:11 ('the mystery of the kingdom') and is rendered 'mystery' in the standard English versions, so 'mysteries' keeps the synoptic resonance and is what the major translations of Thomas print. 'Secrets' would blur the link with the 'hidden' sayings of the incipit, which use a different, native word (ϩⲏⲡ). The corpus parses ⲉⲓ̈- as the focalising converter, which puts the emphasis on the adverbial phrase; English expresses that with a cleft, as Block A does for focalising forms (THOM-12) and Block B at THOM-49.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϣⲙ̄ⲙⲟ 'stranger, guest'; ϩⲟⲙⲧ 'copper, money'; ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ 'bride'; ⲉϣⲱⲧ 'merchant'; G1173 (δεῖπνον), G1713 (ἔμπορος), G2968 (κώμη), G5117 (τόπος)

entries.literal: strangers/guests; dinner; money against merchants; village; be married; buyers; merchants; the places of my Father
entries.standardEnglish: 'guests', 'claims against some merchants', 'farm' or 'estate' for ⲕⲱⲙⲏ, 'businessmen and merchants'
entries.wohChoice: 'guests' (ϣⲙ̄ⲙⲟ, the invitees); 'dinner'; 'money due from some merchants'; 'village' for ⲕⲱⲙⲏ (as at THOM-31); 'is going to be married'; 'Buyers and [merchants will] not [enter] the places of my Father' (plural kept; Greek ⲉⲙⲡⲟⲣⲟⲥ and native ⲉϣⲟⲧⲉ both 'merchants').
entries.rationale: ϣⲙ̄ⲙⲟ means 'stranger' and, in hospitality contexts, 'guest'; the people invited to the dinner are guests, and 'strangers' would mislead. ⲕⲱⲙⲏ is 'village', the rendering already used at THOM-31, and 'farm' or 'estate' interpret the purchase; 'money due from' renders the Coptic 'copper/money against some merchants' without the legal register of 'claims'. The closing line keeps the plural ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ as 'the places' under the topos entry, and renders both merchant words 'merchants' because English has no natural pair; the loan/native contrast is recorded here and the speaker of the closing line is left open, as in the Coptic.

entries.literal: Lord, there are many around the ϫⲱⲧⲉ, but there is no one in the sickness
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin: 'O lord, there are many around the drinking trough, but there is nothing in the cistern' (emending ϣⲱⲛⲉ)
entries.wohChoice: Manuscript reading kept: 'Lord, there are many around the drinking trough(?), but there is no one in the sickness(?).' '(?)' on both nouns: ϫⲱⲧⲉ is of uncertain meaning, and ϣⲱⲛⲉ 'sickness' does not agree with its feminine article (see rationale). The emendation ϣⲱⲧⲉ 'well, cistern' is given in commentary.
entries.rationale: ϣⲱⲛⲉ is a common, securely attested Coptic word for 'sickness' (Crum s.v.; the same lemma appears in ⲛⲉⲧϣⲱⲛⲉ 'the sick' at THOM-14), so the manuscript reading is lexically clear even though it fits the image poorly; the widely printed 'well' or 'cistern' rests on the conjecture ϣⲱⲧⲉ, which Dilley records as uncertain, and on the Greek saying 'many around the well, no one in the well' reported by Origen (Contra Celsum 8.15-16). The crux rule keeps the manuscript in the line and the emendation in the commentary, and the '(?)' convention is reserved for a word whose meaning cannot be established: that is the case for ϫⲱⲧⲉ, for which 'drinking trough' (Lambdin) is a contextual guess. The vocative 'Lord' and the unnamed speaker ('He said') follow the Coptic. Ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01): the article in ⲧϣⲱⲛⲉ is feminine, but ϣⲱⲛⲉ 'sickness' is masculine (Crum, Coptic Dictionary 571a), while ϣⲱⲧⲉ 'pit, well, cistern' is feminine (Crum 595a); the article therefore supports the emendation, and 'sickness' carries '(?)'.

entries.standardEnglish: 'the bridal chamber' (Lambdin and most translations); 'the wedding hall'
entries.wohChoice: 'the bridal chamber' (75); 'is going to be married' for ⲣ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ (64). ⲙⲁ here is part of a compound and is not rendered 'place'. When Block C reaches logion 104 (Greek ⲛⲩⲙⲫⲱⲛ), the loan/native pair is to be recorded there.
entries.rationale: ⲙⲁ ⲛ̄- + noun is a productive Coptic way of forming nouns of place, and ⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ is the native equivalent of Greek νυμφών 'bridal chamber, wedding hall' (Mt 9:15), so 'bridal chamber' is the standard and lexically exact rendering; a literal 'place of the bride' would make a compound look like a phrase. entries.source: Coptic focalising (second) tenses: second perfect ⲛ̄ⲧⲁ- (77 ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ ×2; 85 ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲁⲇⲁⲙ), second present ⲉ(ⲣⲉ)- (82 ⲉϥϩⲏⲛ), and the cleft sentence ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲩ ⲡⲉ ⲉⲧ- (99)
entries.strongs: Layton, A Coptic Grammar (2000), on the focalising conversion (Polotsky's 'second tenses'); corpus tag CFOC in the lemma aid
entries.partOfSpeech: convention: rendering of focalising conversions and cleft sentences
entries.literal: it is X that (the subject) did / does
entries.standardEnglish: Translations vary between an English cleft, fronting and plain word order for the Coptic second tenses
entries.wohChoice: Where the corpus parses a converter as focalising and the focused element is an adverbial that the saying contrasts, the English uses a cleft: 'It is from me that the All came forth, and it is to me that the All has reached' (77); 'It is from a great power and a great wealth that Adam came into being' (85). This continues the practice at THOM-12 (focalising future) and THOM-62 (focalising present). A Coptic cleft sentence is rendered as a cleft (99 'It is they who will enter'). Ordinary word order is kept where the ⲉ- form is homographic with the circumstantial and the parallel clause uses a plain tense (82), and where a second future follows ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ or ϣⲓⲛⲁ in a purpose clause (91, 98, 114), which is the normal purpose construction and carries no special focus. SURFACE CHANGES from the draft's fronted order at 77 and 85.
entries.rationale: Coptic marks focus grammatically with the second tenses, which English cannot reproduce in its verb forms; the cleft is the English construction that carries the same information structure, and it is how the program rendered the focalising forms at THOM-12 and THOM-62. The draft's fronting at 77 and 85 ('From me the All came forth') reads in English as a stylistic inversion rather than as emphasis, and it would have left Block C inconsistent with Blocks A and B. The second tenses also have uses without contrastive focus (above all after ϫⲉⲕⲁⲁⲥ and ϣⲓⲛⲁ), and the corpus's focalising tag on an ⲉ- form is sometimes a choice between homographs, so the convention limits the cleft to clear cases and records the others in commentary. No lens is involved.

entries.partOfSpeech: convention: refines rule 1 of `restored-text-bracket-and-sigla-convention-thomas-woh` (bracket mapping at morph level)
entries.literal: restored letters belonging to a linking particle, object marker, article, converter or adverb that English does not render
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin (in Layton ed. 1989) brackets the English words that stand on restored letters; most popular translations print restorations silently
entries.wohChoice: Rule 1 of the restored-text convention is applied at the level of the morph, as Block A did ('[then you will] see', THOM-37) and Block B did ('within [you]', THOM-70): an English word is bracketed if the Coptic morph it renders is wholly or partly restored. (a) A restored adverb that is part of a compound verb belongs to that verb's lexeme, so the English verb is bracketed ('[appeared]' THOM-50; '[sold it]' 109). (b) A restored morph that no English word renders produces no bracket: the linking or attributive ⲛ̄ (79, 96), the object marker ⲙ̄- / reflexive ⲙ̄ⲙⲟ= (86, 110), a preposition or indefinite plural article with no English counterpart (102), the existential ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ of possession and the causative ⲧⲣⲉ- (109), and a converter with its resumptive pronoun (97 ⲉⲥ-). Each such restoration is named in the commentary of its unit. (c) No bracket encloses an English word that renders extant letters, including underdotted ones (corrections at 97, 103, 109); adjacent bracketed words share one pair, as at THOM-72 (78 '[man who]', 93 '[pearls to]').
entries.rationale: The bracket rule exists to show which English words stand on restored letters, and it misleads in both directions if a bracket covers an English word that renders extant letters or if a bracket appears where no English word renders anything restored. Reading the convention's 'token' as the whole bound group would bracket phrases such as '[the womb]' (79) or '[the world]' (110), where only a one-letter particle is restored and the noun is fully legible, making intact text look damaged; Block A rejected bracketing for scribal slips on the same ground. The morph-level reading is what Blocks A and B already did (THOM-37, 50, 70), so this entry fixes existing practice rather than changing it, and it settles the six Block C cases in one place. Because every unbracketed restoration is named in the commentary, the reader of the apparatus loses no information.

entries.rationale: The title stands after logion 114 in the manuscript and is not part of Jesus's words, so appending it to the English of 114 would make it read as the end of the saying. A numbered unit would break the alignment between the translation and the source file, which deliberately keeps its verse list at 0-114 and stores the title in `source.subscriptTitle`; a chapter-level field mirrors that structure exactly. 'Gospel' renders the loan ⲉⲩⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲓⲟⲛ as the established title word, and ⲡⲕⲁⲧⲁ ('the one according to') is the Coptic way of attaching Greek κατά, rendered 'according to' as in the canonical gospel titles. The incipit names the work 'the hidden sayings' and the subscript names it a gospel; keeping both visible, at 0 and 114, lets the reader see that the manuscript itself uses two designations.

entries.partOfSpeech: nominal sentences; focalising second perfects; imperatives
entries.literal: I am the light which is above all of them … it is to me that the All reached; split a (piece of) wood, I am there; lift the stone up
entries.standardEnglish: 'the light which is above them all', 'the All', 'extend' or 'reach' for the first ⲡⲱϩ; 'Split a piece of wood, and I am there. Lift up the stone, and you will find me there' (standard translations)
entries.wohChoice: 'I am the light that is above them all. I am the All. It is from me that the All came forth, and it is to me that the All has reached. Split a piece of wood: I am there. Lift up the stone, and you will find me there.' The plural 'them all' keeps the unstated antecedent of ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ. The two second perfects are clefts (SURFACE CHANGE; see `focalising-conversion-cleft-convention-thomas-woh`). ⲡⲱϩ is 'reached' and then 'split', with the pun explained in commentary. The Coptic order (wood, then stone) stands; the Greek order and placement are in commentary.
entries.rationale: Every element of the line is the plain sense of the Coptic: ⲉⲧϩⲓϫⲱⲟⲩ ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ is 'which is upon/above them all', ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ is the substantive 'the All' fixed at logion 2, and ϥⲓ … ⲉϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ is 'lift up'. The only device that English cannot carry is the double use of ⲡⲱϩ, 'reach' in 77a and 'split' in 77b, which most commentators take as the catchword that joined the two halves in Coptic; the Greek of P.Oxy. 1, which attaches 77b to logion 30 and uses σχίζω, cannot have it, so the pun is evidence for the Coptic history of the collection and is explained in commentary rather than forced into the English. The Greek's different order and placement are recorded under the base-text convention, and the line follows the Coptic. 'Has reached' is preferred to 'extended' because it keeps the motion toward the speaker that ϣⲁⲣⲟⲉⲓ 'to me' expresses.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲥⲱϣⲉ 'field, open country'; s.v. ⲕⲁϣ 'reed'; s.v. ⲕⲓⲙ 'move, be moved'; G3175 (μεγιστάν); cf. Mt 11:7-8; Lk 7:24-25; Mk 6:21 (μεγιστᾶσιν)
entries.literal: to the field / open country; a reed moving by the wind; your magnates
entries.standardEnglish: Mt 11:7 / Lk 7:24 'into the wilderness … a reed shaken by the wind'; 'great men' or 'powerful men' for ⲙⲉⲅⲓⲥⲧⲁⲛⲟⲥ in translations of Thomas
entries.wohChoice: 'Why have you come out to the countryside? To see a reed shaken [by] the wind?'; 'your great men' (78) and 'a great man' / 'the great man' (98) for ⲙⲉⲅⲓⲥⲧⲁⲛⲟⲥ. ⲥⲱϣⲉ remains 'field' where it is a field (21, 109). The synoptic 'wilderness' is not imported.
entries.rationale: ⲥⲱϣⲉ is the open land outside a settlement, so 'field' at 21 and 109 and 'countryside' here are both its plain sense; the synoptic ἔρημος 'wilderness' is a different word, and importing it would harmonise Thomas with Matthew and Luke against the register convention. ⲕⲓⲙ is the verb 'move' of logion 19 and the noun 'movement' of 50, but of a reed in the wind the English idiom is 'shaken', and the concordance is noted in the kim entry rather than forced into an unidiomatic 'moved'. μεγιστάν means 'grandee, magnate' (the word of Mk 6:21), and 'great men' / 'a great man' keeps the same English at both of its Thomas occurrences, so the reader can see that the assassin's victim at 98 belongs to the class mocked at 78; 'powerful man', common in translations of 98, would hide the link. Ratified at sign-off (2026-11-01): the restored ⲉ[ⲃⲟⲗ] belongs to the compound preposition ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲓⲧⲛ̄ 'by' (Crum CD 429b), not to a compound verb with ⲕⲓⲙ, so the bracket stands on '[by]'.

entries.partOfSpeech: suffixed predicate of blessing ('blessed is/are …') with anticipating pronoun
entries.literal: blessed is she, the womb …; blessed are they, those who …
entries.standardEnglish: 'Blessed is the womb … Blessed are those who …' (standard)
entries.wohChoice: 'Blessed' at all three occurrences (79): 'Blessed is the womb that bore you', 'Blessed are those who have heard', 'Blessed is the womb that has not conceived'. The native/loan pair with ⲙⲁⲕⲁⲣⲓⲟⲥ (7, 18, 19, 49, 54, 58, 103) is recorded here and in commentary, not marked in the English.
entries.rationale: ⲛⲁⲓⲁⲧ= is the native Coptic beatitude, the form the Sahidic New Testament uses to translate μακάριος, so 'Blessed' is its exact English and the reader of Lk 11:27-28 will recognise the saying. Rendering it 'Happy' or 'Fortunate' to make the native/loan difference audible would make the English assert a difference of meaning that the two Coptic forms do not have; the difference is one of vocabulary, which the apparatus records. The central beatitudes entry governs the Sermon beatitudes (Mt 5 / Lk 6) and is not cited, because logion 79 parallels Lk 11 and Lk 23 instead.

entries.literal: the word of the father
entries.standardEnglish: 'the word of the Father' (standard translations of Thomas); Lk 11:28 'the word of God'
entries.wohChoice: 'the word of the Father'; λόγος is kept distinct from native ϣⲁϫⲉ 'sayings / words' (`shaje-ethep-hidden-sayings-thomas-woh`) in the apparatus, and 'Father' is capitalised for the divine referent.
entries.rationale: λόγος is 'word', and the singular collective 'the word of the Father' is the plain rendering; it corresponds to Luke's 'the word of God', with Thomas's characteristic 'the Father' in place of 'God'. Thomas otherwise uses native ϣⲁϫⲉ for the sayings of its collection, and the loan appears only here, so recording the difference keeps the reader from assuming that 'the word of the Father' and 'these sayings' (0, 1) are the same term. Capitalising 'Father' follows the eiot entry, because the context (hearing and keeping his word) establishes the divine referent.

entries.strongs: G720 (ἀρνέομαι); G1411 (δύναμις)
entries.literal: let him deny/refuse; power
entries.standardEnglish: 'let him renounce (it)' (81) and 'let him renounce the world' (110) in standard translations; 'power' for δύναμις
entries.wohChoice: ⲁⲣⲛⲁ = 'renounce' at both occurrences: absolute at 81 ('let him renounce'), with object at 110 ('let him renounce the world'). No object is supplied at 81. ⲇⲩⲛⲁⲙⲓⲥ = 'power' (81; 'a great power' 85, as 'great power' at 21).
entries.rationale: ἀρνέομαι covers 'deny, refuse, renounce', and 'renounce' is the sense that fits both a renunciation of power (81) and of the world (110); using one English verb lets the reader see that 110 repeats the shape of 81. The Coptic of 81 has no object, and supplying 'it' would decide whether the powerful one renounces his power or something else, so the English keeps the verb absolute, which English 'renounce' allows. δύναμις is 'power' in every standard translation, and the same English at 21, 81 and 85 keeps the loan recognisable across the collection.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ 'reveal, appear' (with ⲉⲃⲟⲗ 'be manifest'); s.v. ϭⲱⲗⲡ 'uncover, reveal'
entries.literal: become manifest; be uncovered; appear to
entries.standardEnglish: 'manifest', 'revealed', 'disclosed' vary in translations
entries.wohChoice: ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ = 'be manifest' of a state (83 'are manifest', 84 'become manifest'; Block A 5 'made manifest'), 'appear' of an event (Block A 28, Block B 50); ϭⲱⲗⲡ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ = 'be revealed' (83; Block A 5); ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉ- without ⲉⲃⲟⲗ = 'appear to' (108).
entries.rationale: Thomas uses two verbs of disclosure, ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ and ϭⲱⲗⲡ, side by side in logion 5 and again in 83, so the English keeps one word for each ('manifest', 'revealed') to let the reader see the pair. ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ describes either a state of being visible or the event of appearing, and English needs two words for those, as Blocks A and B already used ('made manifest' at 5, 'appeared' at 28 and 50); the choice is made by context and recorded here. At 108 ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ governs ⲉ- 'to' without ⲉⲃⲟⲗ, and 'appear to' keeps it apart from ϭⲱⲗⲡ, which 'will be revealed to him' would blur.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲉⲓⲛⲉ 'likeness'; s.v. ϥⲓ ϩⲁ- 'bear, endure'; s.v. ⲟⲩⲏⲣ 'how much?'; G1504 (εἰκών)
entries.lemma: ⲉⲓⲛⲉ (native); ϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ (Greek loan); ϥⲓ ϩⲁ-; ⲟⲩⲏⲣ
entries.literal: your likeness; your images which came into being before you; you will bear how much
entries.standardEnglish: 'your likeness … your images which came into being before you … how much you will have to bear!' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'In the days when you see your likeness, you rejoice. But when you see your images that came into being before you, which neither die nor become manifest, how much you will bear!' ⲉⲓⲛⲉ 'likeness' and ϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ 'images' kept distinct; 'before you' (temporal sense in context); exclamation rather than question.
entries.rationale: The saying contrasts two words, native ⲉⲓⲛⲉ (the likeness one sees, as in a mirror) and the Greek loan ϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ (the images that pre-exist the hearers), and keeping 'likeness' and 'images' apart is what makes the contrast visible; 'image' is fixed for ϩⲓⲕⲱⲛ by the eikon entry. ϩⲓⲧⲉⲧⲛⲉϩⲏ is literally 'in front of you', which can be spatial or temporal, but the clause 'which neither die nor become manifest' describes something that precedes the hearers' existence, so 'before you' is read temporally and the alternative is noted. ⲟⲩⲏⲣ is an interrogative of quantity that Coptic uses in exclamations, and the exclamation fits the contrast with 'you rejoice'; Lambdin's modal 'will have to bear' is noted but not adopted, because the Coptic has a plain future.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϣⲁ (ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ 'be worthy'); G514 (ἄξιος)
entries.literal: be worthy of; a worthy one
entries.standardEnglish: 'worthy' for both (standard)
entries.wohChoice: 'worthy' for both native ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ and loan ⲁⲝⲓⲟⲥ, as Block B did at 55 and 56: 'the world is not worthy of him' (80, 111), 'he did not become [worthy] of you … had he been worthy' (85), 'women are not worthy of life' (114).
entries.rationale: ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ and ⲁⲝⲓⲟⲥ both mean 'worthy', and at 85 they stand in one sentence with no difference of sense ('he did not become worthy … for had he been worthy'); a second English word such as 'deserving' would invent a contrast. The formula 'the world is not worthy of him' recurs at 56, 80 and 111, and the same English lets the reader see that 111 quotes it. The pair is recorded here under the loanword convention, which marks meaningful loan/native pairs in the apparatus rather than in the line.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲁϣⲉ 'hang' (stative ⲟϣⲉ); s.v. ⲟⲩⲟⲓ 'woe'; G5005 (ταλαίπωρος)
entries.literal: hanging on; wretched; woe
entries.standardEnglish: 'Wretched is the body that is dependent upon a body' (Lambdin); 'Woe to the flesh that depends on the soul'
entries.wohChoice: ⲁϣⲉ / ⲟϣⲉ ⲛ̄- = 'depend on' (87, 112); ⲧⲁⲗⲁⲓⲡⲱⲣⲟⲥ = 'wretched' (87); ⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓ = 'woe' (102, 112).
entries.rationale: ⲁϣⲉ is 'hang', and with ⲛ̄- it is the idiom 'hang on, depend on'; 'depend on' is the established rendering and avoids the image of a body literally hanging. The same English at 87 and 112 shows that the two sayings are built on one verb, with Greek ταλαίπωρος 'wretched' (the word of Rom 7:24) in one and native ⲟⲩⲟⲓ 'woe' in the other. 'Woe' for ⲟⲩⲟⲓ also matches the woe against the Pharisees at 102.

entries.strongs: G32 (ἄγγελος); G4396 (προφήτης)
entries.literal: the angels/messengers are coming to you with the prophets
entries.standardEnglish: 'The angels and the prophets will come to you' (standard translations)
entries.wohChoice: 'The angels and the prophets are coming to you'. ⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ = 'angels', as 'a righteous angel' at THOM-13; the sense 'messengers' is recorded in commentary, not printed. 'what you have' (ⲛⲉⲧⲉⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲏⲧⲛ̄ⲥⲉ, contrasting ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲡⲱⲟⲩ 'what is theirs'); 'what is in your hands'; 'say to yourselves'.
entries.rationale: ἄγγελος means both 'messenger' and 'angel', and the standard translations of this saying print 'angels'; the program rendered the same loan 'angel' at logion 13, where the comparison is with a heavenly being, and one English word for one loan keeps Thomas consistent. The pairing with 'prophets' who come to the hearers has led some commentators to think of human envoys, and that reading is stated in the commentary so that the line does not hide the lexical range. The program's Hebrew convention 'messenger' for malʾāḵ belongs to a different source word and is not carried into this Greek loan, which is also why any Wheel of Heaven reading of the saying is kept in a separate speculative entry and out of the line.

entries.source: Thomas 88 (ⲛ̄ⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ ⲛⲏⲩ ϣⲁⲣⲱⲧⲛ̄ ⲙⲛ̄ⲛ̄ⲡⲣⲟⲫⲏⲧⲏⲥ … ⲁϣ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲛⲏⲩ ⲛ̄ⲥⲉϫⲓⲡⲉⲧⲉⲡⲱⲟⲩ)
entries.partOfSpeech: interpretive reading recorded in the apparatus (no effect on the English)
entries.literal: the angels are coming to you with the prophets … on what day will they come and take what is theirs?
entries.standardEnglish: Mainstream readings: eschatological messengers who bring the hearers what belongs to them; or itinerant envoys of the early communities, received and provided for; the closing question as the expectation of their return
entries.wohChoice: No effect on any English line. The entry records one interpretive resonance a Wheel of Heaven reader will notice: Thomas pairs ⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ with prophets as visitors who come to the hearers, give them what is theirs, and will come again to take what is theirs; this can be read alongside the canon's account of messengers sent by the Elohim and of the prophets they instructed. It appears once, in a commentary paragraph of THOM-88 labelled 'Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation)', after the mainstream reading.
entries.rationale: Logion 88 does not say who sends the angels and prophets, where they come from, or what 'what is yours' and 'what is theirs' are, and the canon does not cite the saying; reading the visitors as envoys of the Elohim is an interpretive synthesis that goes beyond what Thomas or any single source states, which is the definition of `speculative`. The English line keeps 'angels', the program's rendering of this loan at logion 13, so the lens cannot be read off the translation, and the commentary states the mainstream readings first. The entry exists so that the single point at which the lens touches Block C is listed in one auditable place and can be removed with one decision: if the reviewer declines it, delete the labelled last paragraph of the THOM-88 notes and drop this id from its glossaryRefs; nothing else depends on it. Logion 77 ('I am the light that is above them all') was considered and deliberately left without a lens paragraph, to keep the use sparing. Ratified at human sign-off on 2026-11-01 (zarazinsfuss), apparatus only.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲧⲁⲙⲓⲟ 'make, create'; cf. Lk 11:40 ὁ ποιήσας (ποιέω G4160)
entries.literal: the one who made the inside … the one who made the outside
entries.standardEnglish: 'he who made the inside is the same one who made the outside' (standard translations); Lk 11:40 'Did not the one who made the outside make the inside also?'
entries.wohChoice: 'made' at both occurrences; not 'created'. 'the outside / the inside' as at THOM-22.
entries.rationale: ⲧⲁⲙⲓⲟ is the ordinary Coptic verb 'make', also used for creation, and in a saying about washing a cup the household sense is the one in view; Luke's ποιέω is likewise 'make'. 'Created' would give the saying a theological weight the image does not require, and in this program creator vocabulary carries the project's lens, so the neutral 'made' keeps the line clear of it. The English therefore follows the normalised reading, as Blocks A and B did for normalisation-only corrections, but because the line depends on reading one written form as another it is labelled `inferred` rather than treated as a plain lexical fact. The proverb is attested in Greek literature (Lucian, Timon 14) and was later told among the Aesopic fables, which confirms the sense without deciding how the manuscript spelled the word.

entries.wohChoice: '[Blessed] is the man who knows [in which] part the robbers are coming in, so that [he] may rise, gather his [domain], and gird his loins [before] they come in.' ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ = 'domain' here, extending by its own criterion the logion-21 exception of `mntero-the-kingdom-thomas-woh` (SURFACE CHANGE from the draft's '[kingdom]'); ⲙⲉⲣⲟⲥ = 'part' (unspecified); ⲥⲱⲟⲩϩ = 'gather'; bracket narrowed to '[he] may' (ⲛⲁ extant).
entries.rationale: The mntero entry renders ⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟ 'domain' in the householder image of logion 21, where the word describes a man's own property, and logion 103 is the same image: the same ⲗⲏⲥⲧⲏⲥ 'robbers', the same girding of the loins (ⲙⲟⲩⲣ … ⲉϫⲛ̄ ϯⲡⲉ), and the same synoptic background (Lk 12:39 / Mt 24:43); the standard English translation (Lambdin) reads 'domain' at both places. 'Gather his kingdom' would turn the householder into an allegory of the kingdom of the Father that the Coptic does not mark, while the lexical identity of the word is kept visible in commentary. The decision is `inferred` because it rests on a judgement about the image rather than on the lexicon, and it is escalated for review because it widens a ratified exception; 'part' for ⲙⲉⲣⲟⲥ keeps the text's silence about whether the night or the house is meant.

entries.literal: when the bridegroom comes out of the bridal chamber; or in what have they prevailed over me
entries.standardEnglish: 'when the bridegroom leaves the bridal chamber' (standard translations); Mk 2:19 'the sons of the bridal chamber' / 'wedding guests'
entries.wohChoice: ⲛⲩⲙⲫⲱⲛ = 'the bridal chamber', the same English as native ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ at 75; the loan/native pair is recorded in the apparatus, not split in the line. ⲛⲩⲙⲫⲓⲟⲥ = 'the bridegroom' (matthew-woh 25). 'or in what have I been overcome?' (impersonal active rendered passive). The order pray/fast and fast/pray kept as written.
entries.rationale: νυμφών is 'bridal chamber, wedding hall', and ⲡⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ, literally 'the place of the bride', is its native Coptic equivalent, so the two words mean the same thing; rendering one of them 'wedding hall' would make the English assert a difference the Coptic does not make, which the loanword convention avoids (compare 'place' for ⲧⲟⲡⲟⲥ / ⲙⲁ and 'worthy' for ⲁⲝⲓⲟⲥ / ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ). The pair is nevertheless recorded, because Thomas uses both and the later Valentinian rite of the 'bridal chamber' makes the term sensitive; as at 75, the commentary states that the rendering does not import that rite. The impersonal ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲩϫⲣⲟ ⲉⲣⲟⲉⲓ ('they have prevailed over me') is rendered as a passive, the usual English for the Coptic impersonal plural.

entries.literal: whoever will know the father and the mother will be called the son of a prostitute
entries.standardEnglish: 'will be called the son of a harlot' (Lambdin); 'the child of a whore' or 'of a prostitute' in other translations
entries.wohChoice: 'Whoever knows the father and the mother will be called the son of a whore.' 'father' and 'mother' lower case (referent unresolved); 'son' under the filial rule; 'whore' for ⲡⲟⲣⲛⲏ. The hard saying is kept as written.
entries.rationale: The saying does not say whose father and mother are meant (the hearer's parents, the divine Father and a heavenly Mother, or both are all proposed), and the eiot entry reserves the capital for a context that establishes the divine Father, so lower case leaves the referent open. πόρνη is 'prostitute', and in the phrase 'the son of a …' it is an insult; 'whore' keeps that register in modern English, where 'harlot' is archaic and 'prostitute' clinical. 'Son' follows the book-wide filial rule ratified at Block A sign-off.

entries.standardEnglish: 'you will become the sons of man' (Lambdin); 'children of humanity' (other translations)
entries.wohChoice: 'you will become sons of man', lower case: plural and without article, so the central Son-of-Man title convention (singular, 86) does not apply; 'sons' under the filial rule. The possible link to 86 (singular ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ with article) is noted in commentary, not marked in the English.
entries.rationale: The central Son-of-Man entry governs the singular title ⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ / ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, and logion 106 has neither the singular nor the article on ϣⲏⲣⲉ, so capitalising it would turn a predicate into a title the Coptic does not mark. 'Sons' follows the ratified filial rule, and 'man' renders singular ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ, which distinguishes the phrase from 28's 'the sons of men' with plural ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ. Because ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ has the article, some readers take the phrase as 'sons of the Man' and connect it with 86; the English keeps the plain wording and the commentary states the possibility.

entries.literal: a man, a shepherd; one of them went astray, it being the great one; when he had toiled; I love you more than the ninety-nine
entries.standardEnglish: 'a shepherd … the largest … When he had gone to such trouble … I care for you more than the ninety-nine' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'a man, a shepherd' (apposition, as 'a man, a merchant' at 76); 'it was the largest'; 'Having toiled'; 'I love you more than the ninety-nine'. 'The kingdom', not 'of the Father'. Supplied letter and rasura rendered silently.
entries.rationale: The appositive ⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛ̄ϣⲱⲥ is kept as at 76 ('a man, a merchant') under the rome entry, so that Thomas's parable openings read alike. ϯⲟⲩⲟϣⲕ is the stative of ⲟⲩⲱϣ 'wish, want, love', and 'I love you' gives the affective sense the shepherd's words require; 'I care for you' (Lambdin) and 'I want you' are recorded in commentary. ϩⲓⲥⲉ is rendered 'toiled' here because the clause describes the effort of the search; the hise entry records the word's range ('suffered' at 58, 'trouble' at 97). The Thomas-specific details (the largest sheep; love 'more than the ninety-nine') are what distinguish this version from Matthew and Luke, and they stay in the line.

entries.literal: whoever will drink from my mouth will become like me; I myself will become (it), he being it
entries.standardEnglish: 'He who will drink from my mouth will become like me. I myself shall become he' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'Whoever drinks from my mouth will become like me; I myself will become he, and the hidden things will appear to him.' Literal 'drinks from my mouth' (not 'my teaching'); 'I myself will become he'; 'the hidden things' (`shaje-ethep-hidden-sayings-thomas-woh`); 'appear to' (`ouonh-ebol-bolp-ebol-manifest-revealed-appear-thomas-woh`).
entries.rationale: The image of drinking from Jesus's mouth continues the drinking of logion 13 ('you have drunk … from the bubbling spring') and is kept literal, because paraphrasing it as 'my teaching' would decide its meaning for the reader. ⲁⲛⲟⲕ ϩⲱ ϯⲛⲁϣⲱⲡⲉ ⲉⲛⲧⲟϥ ⲡⲉ ends in a circumstantial nominal sentence ('he being it'), whose closest English is 'I myself will become he', the standard rendering; 'I will become him' is less exact grammatically. The Lycopolitan future relative ⲡⲉⲧⲁ- is rendered with the generic English present 'whoever drinks', as elsewhere in the collection.

entries.literal: a treasure hidden, he being ignorant of it; he came ploughing; he began to give money at interest to those he wished
entries.standardEnglish: 'a [hidden] treasure in his field without knowing it … He began to lend money at interest to whomever he wished' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'a [hidden] treasure in his field, [being] unaware of it … The son [did] not know; he took that field and [sold it]. And the one [who] bought it came plowing; [he found] the treasure, and he began to lend money at interest to [those whom] he wished.' 'treasure' (as at 76); 'plowing'; the moneylending ending kept against 95. Brackets narrowed at 'the one [who]' and 'to [those whom]' (SURFACE CHANGE: ⲡ̣ and ⲛ̣ are extant).
entries.rationale: Thomas's parable differs from Mt 13:44 in following the treasure through three owners and in ending with the finder becoming a moneylender, which contradicts the prohibition at 95; the convention for hard sayings keeps that ending, and the shared English 'lend money at interest' makes the tension visible. ⲁϩⲟ is 'treasure' as at 76, and ϩⲏⲡ 'hidden' keeps the collection's 'hidden' vocabulary. The two bracket corrections apply the morph rule: the article ⲡ̣ ('the one') and the preposition ⲛ̣ ('to') are extant, underdotted letters, so the English words that render them stand outside the brackets.

entries.partOfSpeech: relative stative used verbally and substantivally; focalising present after οὐχ ὅτι
entries.literal: the one living from the living one will not see death; not that Jesus says: whoever will find himself, the world is not worthy of him
entries.standardEnglish: 'And the one who lives from the living one will not see death. Does not Jesus say, "Whoever finds himself is superior to the world"?' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'The heavens will be rolled up, and the earth, in your presence, and the one who lives from the living one will not see death. Does not Jesus say, 'Whoever finds himself, the world is not worthy of him'?' The first ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ is verbal ('the one who lives from'), the second the substantive 'the living one' (lower case); 'will not see death' (ⲛⲁⲩ); the closing clause is a rhetorical question, printed without any gloss marking in the line.
entries.rationale: The phrase ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲛϩ repeats one form, but the first is construed with ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄- 'from', which requires a verbal reading ('lives from'), while the second is the substantive 'the living one' fixed by the etonh entry; strict concordance ('the living one from the living one') would hide that construction. The closing clause, introduced by Greek οὐχ ὅτι with a focalising present and speaking of Jesus in the third person, is widely taken as a comment added in transmission that quotes the substance of 56/80; the rhetorical question 'Does not Jesus say …?' is the standard rendering, but οὐχ ὅτι elsewhere means 'not that …', so the parse takes a position and the entry is `inferred`. Marking the clause as a gloss in the line would be a claim about the text's history, which belongs to the apparatus, so the English prints the words and the commentary explains them.

entries.literal: the kingdom, it is coming on what day? it is not coming by a looking-out; the kingdom of the father is spread out upon the earth and people do not see it
entries.standardEnglish: 'It will not come by waiting for it … the kingdom of the father is spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: 'The kingdom, on what day will it come? It will not come by watching out for it. They will not say, 'Behold, here,' or 'Behold, there.' Rather, the kingdom of the Father is spread out upon the earth, and people do not see it.' No speech formula supplied for the answer (as at 43); topicalised subject kept; ϭⲱϣⲧ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ = 'watching out for' (as at 21, 51).
entries.rationale: The answer has no ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ in the Coptic, and the register convention supplies none, as Block B ruled at 43. ϩⲛ̄ⲟⲩϭⲱϣⲧ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ uses the noun of the verb rendered 'watch out for' at 21 and 51 (`goosht-look-watch-thomas-woh`), and the same English keeps the disciples' question at 51 and this reply connected; English 'watch out for' requires the object 'it', which resolves the absolute noun without adding content. 'Spread out upon the earth' renders ⲡⲱⲣϣ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ and ⲕⲁϩ under the world/earth entry, and plural ⲣ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ is 'people', as at 16.

entries.literal: I will draw her in order that I may make her male … a living spirit resembling you males; every woman who will make herself male
entries.standardEnglish: 'I myself shall lead her in order to make her male, so that she too may become a living spirit resembling you males. For every woman who will make herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven' (Lambdin)
entries.wohChoice: Manuscript reading kept: 'Let Mariham go out from among us, for women are not worthy of life … Behold, I myself will lead her, so that I may make her male, so that she too may become a living spirit resembling you males. For every woman who makes herself male will enter the kingdom of the heavens.' Not softened, not glossed in the line; 'lead' for ⲥⲱⲕ; lower-case 'living spirit'; 'the kingdom of the heavens' (central).
entries.rationale: ⲉⲉⲓⲛⲁⲁⲥ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩⲧ and ⲉⲥⲛⲁⲁⲥ ⲛ̄ϩⲟⲟⲩⲧ are unambiguous ('make her male', 'makes herself male'), and the convention for hard sayings forbids softening them (for instance to 'make her whole' or 'make her like you'); the interpretations, which read the image against logion 22 and against ancient language in which becoming male describes moving from the perishable to the perfect, belong in commentary. ⲥⲱⲕ is 'draw, lead', and 'lead' gives the sense of guidance that the clause requires; 'draw' is noted. 'A living spirit' is lower case under the pneuma and etonh entries, since the phrase describes what she will become and is not a title.
